For how to do it, see Analysis files, history, and recovery. <details <summary View before and after recovery, and the history</summary </details Notes on the cases These cases were actually run on 2026-11-05; Cases 1–4 used v8/v9 and Case 5 used v10. The data, code, logs, and outputs were all saved, and the statistical results and files were checked. The environment record gives exact package versions and rebuild notes, but that is not a complete environment archive, and this round did not verify a dependency reinstall; for more scope and limits, see Current scope and limits in the Scientific Figures guide.

en.title: Virtual cell perturbation prediction benchmark
en.description: Use SciForge to organize the data contract, runs, scoring, failure analysis, and reruns for an external perturbation prediction model.
en.body: Virtual cell perturbation prediction benchmark This case is for researchers who already have a perturbation prediction model and a compute environment. SciForge organizes the data, code, run records, results, evidence, and human review; the prediction capability comes from the external model you connect. The offline fixture, model adapter, and full continuous screenshots are not yet fully verified in the current version. This page publishes an implementable evaluation contract and operating boundaries; it does not present them as an "out-of-the-box built-in virtual cell model." Evaluation task The 2026 Virtual Cell Challenge task is zero-shot cross-cell-background prediction: the model receives unperturbed baseline cells and CRISPRi knockdown target genes, and predicts post-perturbation expression profiles in cell backgrounds it has not seen before. For the official description, see Arc Institute's task overview. This tutorial focuses on four common risks: - The model sees the sealed ground truth before prediction, causing data leakage - Data, weight, or environment drift makes results impossible to rerun - The output shape is valid but gene order, value type, or labels are wrong - Only the overall score is reported, hiding consistent failures on specific backgrounds or perturbations Choose a path first Path Purpose Ground truth and scoring External effects --- --- --- --- A. Offline reproduction demo After preparing offline data, walk through prediction, sealing, local scoring, and rerun Requires independently sealed validation data prepared in advance; this site does not yet provide a verified fixture, and it is not the official held-out ground truth No upload by default; a small local CPU slice works B. VCC 2026 online path Assemble the official inputs and run pre-submission checks Run the official CLI preflight locally; final scoring happens on the official server Downloads, sign-ins, uploads, and submissions each require separate confirmation The two paths can share the prediction artifact contract, but they must not mix ground truth or scoring claims. When you cannot determine the path, stop. Workspace boundaries in SciForge Start by inspecting the protocol, data, model, and existing runs in the SciForge Files panel; do not launch a full prediction right away. Figure 1: The Files panel is used to check the current workspace and key inputs; this feature screenshot is not a completed benchmark run. Suggested layout: text virtual-cell-benchmark/ ├── protocol/ │ ├── evaluation-plan.md │ ├── data-contract.yaml │ └── split-manifest.json ├── data/ │ ├── inputs/ │ └── sealed-reference/ Path A only ├── models/ │ ├── baseline/ │ └── external-adapter/ ├── scripts/ │ ├── validate_inputs.py │ ├── run_prediction.py │ ├── validate_prediction.py │ ├── evaluate_offline.py Path A only │ └── analyze_failures.py └── runs/<run-id / ├── run-manifest.json ├── environment-lock. ├── logs/ ├── predictions/ ├── validation/ ├── metrics/ ├── figures/ └── dossier/ run-manifest.json is the core index. At minimum it records the path type, input hashes, code commit, model and weight hashes, environment, device, random seed, prediction hash, command, return code, and timestamp. Official output contract snapshot As of 2026-09-04, the full submission contract given by the official VCC CLI documentation includes: Contract item Official requirement Local check --- ---: --- Perturbations × cells per condition × backgrounds 300 × 400 × 3 Exact counts per background and per perturbation Total predicted cells 360,000 Check obs row count and duplicate keys Gene dimension 18,533 Gene set, order, and uniqueness Values Raw, non-negative integer counts Reject log-normalized, scaled, or negative values Control cells Should not be included Scan for non-targeting control labels Local preflight vcc prep --dry-run Save the CLI version, command, return code, and full output The official bundle downloaded at run time and the VCC CLI documentation are the final authority; if the CLI disagrees with this page, stop and update the protocol. Full task prompt text Please organize a reproducible virtual cell perturbation prediction evaluation in the current workspace. Goal: use unperturbed baseline cells and the given knockdown target genes to generate post-perturbation expression predictions, and pin the data, model, environment, runs, and results into a reviewable evidence chain. First determine the path from the workspace: - Path A: offline reproduction fixture, where local scoring can run after predictions are sealed. - Path B: official VCC 2026, where locally you only run contract checks and vcc prep --dry-run. - If you cannot determine the path, stop. Do not guess or mix the two paths. Execution requirements: 1. Inspect Git, data, model code, weights, environment, and evaluation scripts in read-only mode. 2. Generate an input inventory and hash manifest, separating what the model can see from what it cannot. 3. Before the first prediction, fix the metrics, aggregation rules, and failure conditions. 4. Run a small-sample dry run first, and check shape, gene order, labels, value types, device, and random seed. 5. Once that passes, generate predictions and record the command, arguments, environment, resources, return code, and prediction hash. 6. For path A, only read the sealed fixture after predictions are sealed. 7. For path B, run only vcc prep --dry-run; stop and confirm before any download, sign-in, upload, or submission. 8. Break down error by background, target gene, expression range, and metric component; do not report only the overall score. 9. Add the protocol, inputs, runs, predictions, validation, metrics, failures, and limitations to the Evidence DAG. 10. Rerun from a clean environment and generate a Research Dossier. Without my confirmation, do not download weights, install dependencies, sign in to external services, submit compute jobs, or upload data. If the input contract, gene space, scoring path, or evaluation script cannot be verified, stop immediately. Execution phases 1. Pre-register the protocol Create evaluation-plan.md before the first prediction, and freeze the data split, primary metrics, auxiliary metrics, aggregation rules, model-visible content, and stop conditions. The file time and Git record must predate the prediction output. 2. Pin the model and environment Record the code commit, weight hashes, license, environment lockfile, device, and random seed. Do not silently download new weights, swap models, or change data preprocessing. When you need an external GPU or a lab cluster, you can submit the job to your own remote environment through the Terminal; the remote side still uses the same output contract. 3. Small-sample dry run Check on the smallest slice: - Input and output shape - Gene ID set and order - Perturbation and background labels - Cells per condition - Non-negative integer counts - Sparse storage and peak memory - Device, random seed, and return code If any hard contract check fails, do not proceed to the full prediction. 4. Run and seal predictions As soon as the full prediction finishes, compute its hash, write it into the run manifest, and put the logs, return code, and resource information under the same run-id . An original run must not be overwritten by a later rerun. 5A. Offline scoring Only after predictions are sealed may you open the sealed fixture and score with the frozen evaluation script. If the reference was read by the model or an analysis script before sealing, mark that run as invalid and start over in a new workspace. 5B. Official preflight Run vcc prep --dry-run with the current official CLI. Passing the preflight does not mean you have submitted. Any sign-in, packaged upload, or formal submission is an external operation: show the target, files, size, and purpose, and get user confirmation. Stratified analysis and evidence review Divide the results into at least four layers: 1. Contract layer : whether files, shape, gene order, count type, and labels are correct. 2. Metric layer : report every component, the overall score, and the aggregation rules. 3. Stratified layer : check performance by background, perturbation, expression strength, and gene abundance. 4. Biology layer : label pathway or cell-state interpretations as hypotheses, and do not write scores directly as mechanistic conclusions. Recommended figures include component metrics, a dot plot stratified by background, perturbation-level error ranking, a differential expression comparison of observed versus predicted values, and an in-depth profile of at least one failure condition. Finally, in SciForge, organize the protocol, inputs, runs, predictions, metrics, failure cases, and limitations into the research dossier. Figure 3: The Research Dossier aggregates the research narrative, versions, confidence, and limitations; continuous screenshots from the same benchmark session still need to be captured before the case is officially published. When you must stop Problem Risk Handling --- --- --- Background labels unknown or swapped Predictions that look valid on the wrong background Check against a fixed mapping and stop immediately Same gene set but a different order Distorted metrics Check both the set and the order before prediction and scoring Output is normalized or scaled values Violates the raw count contract Verify non-negativity, integer values, and provenance; stop on failure Wrong cell count per perturbation Condition weights shift Verify exact counts per background and per perturbation Environment or weight drift Reruns are not comparable Create a new run-id and produce a difference report Path B preparing an upload Data leaves the local machine Show the target and files, and wait for user confirmation Completion criteria These items are the acceptance criteria for a later integration run; this page does not provide proof of a completed prediction, scoring, and rerun. - Path A/B is clear and the two are not mixed - The protocol predates the first prediction - Input, code, weight, environment, and prediction hashes are all present - All hard contracts pass in the dry run - The overall score and stratified failures are reported together - Rerun differences are recorded and explained - No external upload or submission happened without confirmation Next: Remote resources and collaboration.

en.title: ECCITE-seq cross-scale virtual cell evidence atlas
en.description: Review CRISPR perturbations, multimodal responses, figures, and evidence boundaries in SciForge.
en.body: ECCITE-seq cross-scale virtual cell evidence atlas This case organizes CRISPR perturbation, target annotation, pathways, transcriptional response, protein response, and cell fitness into an inspectable cross-scale evidence chain. SciForge manages the workspace, execution process, figures, evidence, and human review; it is not described as a built-in virtual cell predictor. The five screenshots below come from the current SciForge development build and open real artifacts in a separate cross-scale-data-demo workspace. They verify the artifact browsing path, but they do not claim that the current version has already completed every rerun from the same session. Research question After a designated target gene is CRISPR-perturbed in a specific cell background, what changes in transcription, protein, pathways, and cell fitness? Which data and methods support each conclusion? The case must answer both "what did we get" and "what can we still not say." Differential expression, protein response, or phenotypic association cannot automatically be promoted to a causal mechanism; cross-layer missingness must also be preserved as a result. Final delivery package The following are the acceptance targets for one complete case run. The current screenshots already show data, figure, and report browsing; same-session generation and review of the Evidence DAG, Research Checkpoint, and Research Dossier still need to be confirmed in an actual run. - Data sources, Git commit, file hashes, and environment baseline - A cross-scale perturbation review table that preserves controls and missing states - A set of versioned figures generated from verified derived tables - A quality audit report, run manifest, and artifact inventory - An Evidence DAG linking claims, data, scripts, figures, and limitations - A human-reviewed Research Checkpoint and Research Dossier Verified data snapshot The following is the static baseline of the public demo copy cross-scale-data-demo@0696755 . A real run must recompute these values instead of hard-coding the numbers into scripts. Item Snapshot Runtime check --- ---: --- Total rows in the review table 35 Recomputed from the final TSV Unique target genes 15 Deduplicated after excluding non-targeting controls Perturbation guides / non-targeting controls 27 / 8 Check perturbation type explicitly L1 target and L2 pathway annotation 27/35 Output unmatched identifiers L3 transcriptional response 27/35 measured Separate unmeasured from no significant response L4 protein response 35/35 measured State that the ADT panel has only 4 markers L5 fitness endpoint 27/35 The 8 missing entries must not be zero-filled Quality checks 42 pass, 1 warning The warning points to the L5 missing rate Delivered artifacts 22 Count data, results, figures, scripts, reports, and manifests by category Workspace and artifact contract text cross-scale-data-demo/ ├── data/final/case45_cross_scale_integrated_dataset.tsv ├── data/processed/case45_l0_l5/case45_p0_20260708T1015Z/ └── run-output/ ├── scripts/ │ ├── stage01_source_inventory.py │ ├── stage02_reconstruct_dataset.py │ ├── stage03_quality_audit.py │ ├── stage04_context_expansion.py │ ├── stage05_generate_figures.py │ └── stage06_write_report.py ├── datasets/ ├── results/ ├── figures/ └── reports/case45_local_demo_report.md Every Stage should record its inputs, outputs, return code, and stop conditions. If the quality audit fails, do not continue to conclusion figures; figures must come from verified derived tables; and the final report must not hide warnings or unverified items. Figure 1: SciForge keeps the case workspace and task on the left, while the Files panel on the right expands the run-output/figures artifact tree. Permissions and baseline before you start This case creates scripts, tables, figures, and research records, so it requires "Can modify working directory"; the read-only sandbox from Getting started does not apply. Before you start, you must: 1. Use a case copy that can be published and redistributed. 2. Check git status --short and record the baseline commit. 3. Inventory the input files and record hashes, sources, and license boundaries. 4. Review the agent plan, output paths, and dependency requirements. 5. Do not install dependencies or access unlisted external services without confirmation. Full task prompt text Please complete one reviewable ECCITE-seq cross-scale perturbation analysis in the current workspace. Research question: compare the designated target genes against non-targeting controls and inspect the evidence relationships among target annotation, pathways, transcriptional response, protein response, and cell fitness. Execution requirements: 1. Check Git status first, inventory the data, scripts, and existing artifacts, and do not overwrite the original files. 2. Present the plan, output paths, and data quality checks before you start writing. 3. Preserve non-targeting controls and missing data; do not automatically fill missing values with zeros. 4. Produce a traceable perturbation review table that lists the source and transformation for each row. 5. Generate cross-layer coverage figures and key response figures from the review table, and save the figure versions. 6. Link claims, data, methods, figures, and limitations into the Evidence DAG. 7. Generate a Research Checkpoint and a Research Dossier, and list the causal conclusions that are not yet supported. Unless I explicitly allow it, do not install dependencies, do not access unlisted external services, and do not modify the raw data. Mark any data or conclusion you cannot verify as "unverified". Phase 1: Freeze sources and inspect the data The agent first inventories the data, scripts, and existing artifacts, then checks perturbation labels, controls, cell backgrounds, measured modalities, and missing values. The completion signal here is not a one-line "checks passed," but an inventory, a hash manifest, and a quality audit report you can open. Check specifically: - Non-targeting controls are not lost in a join or filter - missing is not conflated with the numeric value 0 - "Not measured" and "measured with no significant response" are expressed separately - Every external annotation records the provider, query conditions, and access date Figure 2: Viewing L0–L5 coverage and measurement status in SciForge; the workspace and task context remain in frame. Phase 2: Assemble the perturbation review table Connect perturbations, target annotation, pathways, and multimodal responses into one row-by-row traceable table. Recompute the row count, unique target gene count, control count, and per-layer coverage, and output the list of unmatched identifiers. If you only have a ready-made derived table without the complete raw counts, you must downgrade the task to "a traceable review of the existing derived results," and you must not claim that the full differential expression analysis was redone. Phase 3: Generate and inspect versioned figures All figures are generated from derived tables that passed the audit, and each records its input hash, script, parameters, and figure version. The same inputs and recipe should rebuild the same result. Figure 3: The file preview shows both the figure and the actual artifact path, so you can trace a result back to its input. When reading L3 and L4, do not give priority to the layer that "matches expectations better." A direction mismatch may come from time scale, measurement noise, or the coverage limits of the 4-marker ADT panel, and it should be preserved as a cross-layer separation result. Figure 4: Causal readiness, L3/L4 overlap, and the L5 effect distribution are inspected together in SciForge; this figure cannot support a causal claim on its own. Phase 4: Review the evidence and lock down delivery Connect each key claim to the original records, derived table, method script, and figure. Counter-evidence, missingness, and limitations should also become evidence nodes rather than being deleted from the final narrative. After the review passes: 1. Open Changes to verify the write scope. 2. Save an Artifact Version for the figures and key files. 3. Create a Research Checkpoint. 4. Record the research question, inputs, methods, results, limitations, and rerun procedure in the Research Dossier. Figure 5: The first screen of the final report shows stage status, the data baseline, the quality audit, and the artifact count. Conclusion writing template text Supported claims: - Which perturbation affected which layer of measurement, in which cell background? - Which original records, derived tables, methods, and figures directly support it? Candidate explanations: - Which pathway or mechanism could explain the result? - What assumptions does it depend on, and what validation is still missing? Claims that cannot be supported: - Why is the current data insufficient to support causal, generalized, or clinical conclusions? - What data, experiments, or independent reproduction is needed next? Failure paths and recovery Problem Wrong approach Correct handling --- --- --- L5 missing Fill with 0 and include in the average Keep the missing flag and report total N and evaluable N separately L3/L4 direction mismatch Keep only the layer that matches expectations better Keep the separated result and check the time scale and marker coverage Audit raises an error Keep plotting and write the Dossier Stop at the quality stage and rerun from the affected Stage after fixing External annotation unavailable Silently switch provider Use a frozen snapshot or stop, and flag freshness Raw counts incomplete Claim the full analysis was redone Downgrade to a traceable review of the existing derived table Completion criteria Use the following to accept your own run; they do not mean this page has already completed all continuous verification. - Baseline commit, input hashes, and environment records are available - The 35-row review table, 15 target genes, and 8 controls can be recomputed - Missing states and warnings are not hidden - Figures trace back to verified derived tables and generation scripts - Key claims have an evidence, counter-evidence, or unresolved status - Checkpoint, Dossier, and Git changes are reviewed together Related feature: Evidence & Reproducibility.

en.title: Anchored Comments
en.description: Select a piece of text, leave a comment, and come back to discuss and check it in place.
en.body: Anchored Comments Select a piece of text in a research record to leave a question, a suggested change, or review feedback on it. The comment keeps the original text and its position, so you can check back later. Add a comment 1. In Extensions & marketplace, install and enable a compatible Anchored Comments plugin. 2. Open Research record , and drag to select text within a single entry. 3. Click Add comment , and check the selected text shown in the panel and the research-record entry it belongs to. 4. Write your feedback and click Save . Discuss selection opens a chat draft that carries the selected text. To save it as a comment, use Add comment . If the panel already holds unsaved content, a new selection asks whether to keep or replace the draft. View, edit, and delete You can ask the Agent to list, view, or update the comments that already exist in the current workspace. The panel is mainly for creating new comments; to change an existing one, say in the session which comment to update and what to change. Deleting a comment requires confirmation. Comments are stored in the workspace and do not change the commented source file. After you switch projects, select the content you want to comment on again. Screenshots and feedback A screenshot needs a separate action; saving text does not take one automatically. The current app view can be saved only when the app supports screenshots and screenshot permission has been granted. Before capturing, check the screen for accounts, tokens, or other sensitive information. Submitting feedback to an external service also needs separate confirmation. If no feedback service is configured, comments can only be saved and discussed locally. Tips - After the original text changes, re-check the quotation and its position. - Comments belong to the current workspace. Before sharing a project, check the comments and screenshots for content you do not want to share. - The current plugin version is 0.2.1 . For installation requirements and version notes, see Version & Compatibility. Related: Agent workflows, Plugin license terms.

en.title: Artifact Versions
en.description: Save independent versions of a single artifact such as a figure or data file, and compare or restore them at any time.
en.body: Artifact Versions Artifact Versions helps you keep different versions of the same figure, the same dataset, or any other file. Every save leaves an independent version, so you can view, compare, and restore it. After you change a workspace file, you need to save the artifact version again for this result to stay in the history. You can review the research process through Research Checkpoints, and check how a conclusion relates to its sources in Evidence DAG. Opening it - Entry: the Artifacts area of the workbench research summary lists recent artifacts; after selecting an entry, view its versions in the Research panel on the right. - Target: a single artifact in the current workspace, such as a figure, data, log, or code file. - Prerequisite: the session is bound to a workspace, and the Agent or the plugin that produced the artifact has already saved an artifact version. Save and check versions 1. Produce a figure or data in a task, and confirm the actual file is in the current workspace. 2. Have the Agent save an independent version of this artifact, and associate the inputs and related files used to produce it. 3. Find the artifact in the Artifacts list, open it, and check the currently selected version, the content digest, and the related files. 4. After changing the artifact, save again. In the Versions area of the research dossier, choose the two versions to compare, and check the differences in content and generation information. 5. When you need an older result, choose the historical version and restore it as a new version. Restoring keeps the existing history; afterwards, check the new version and the actual file state. Export and import Before delivery, explicitly choose the artifact versions to export in the research dossier, then export a Bundle. Exporting writes files, and the interface asks for confirmation first. Check that all the versions and related files the bundle needs are present, and that they are all allowed to be accessed and exported; if any required version is not visible or not allowed to be exported, the whole export fails. Validate the Bundle before importing it in the target workspace. Importing adds version records; a package with missing dependencies, inconsistent history, or damaged content is rejected. Before sharing, also check the bundle for data that should not be sent out. Tips - Only artifacts that have been saved appear in the version list. Scientific Figures keeps its own figure history and does not register it here automatically; when you need a link, save an artifact version separately. - Some versions reference workspace files. After a file is moved, changed, or deleted, viewing it may report a changed or missing source; check the actual file first. - Viewing, comparing, restoring, and importing are all limited by version access permissions. An entry in the history list may also be impossible to open or export. - A version record does not replace scientific review of the result; before delivery, still check the inputs, the methods, and the conclusions. Related pages - Evidence & Reproducibility: the group overview and the recommended record chain. - Research Dossier: view, compare, restore, and export selected versions. - Evidence DAG: use versions as the evidence and sources for claims. - Git Checkpoints: save the Git state of the whole workspace. - Workspaces and sessions: how a workspace limits the scope of artifacts.

en.title: Automation and scheduled tasks
en.description: Use scheduled tasks to repeat a single Agent instruction, or use Create Loop to organize multi-step flows.
en.body: Automation and scheduled tasks First verify in an ordinary session that the task completes correctly, then turn it into an automation. Define the output path and the operations that need confirmation up front, so that scheduled repeats do not overwrite files or submit twice. Automation has two entry points: Scheduled tasks is a built-in scheduling capability of the app, not a domain extension; Create Loop is a built-in flow tool for multi-node orchestration. Choose which one Need Entry point --- --- Run a single AI instruction daily, once, at an interval, or manually Scheduled tasks (this page) Connect AI tasks, conditions, HTTP requests, approvals, and subflows Create Loop Create a scheduled task Open Scheduled tasks from the left, click New task , and configure the name, instruction, model, reasoning effort, run time, and workspace in order. Figure 1: A scheduled task puts the task content, model, schedule, and runtime environment in a single configuration table. An instruction suitable for validation: Check the current workspace for newly appeared experiment logs and produce a summary of no more than three items. Do not modify the original logs; save the output to the prearranged reports directory. Scheduled tasks require SciForge to keep running and the computer to be awake at the trigger time. "Keep awake" only prevents suspension while a task is running; it cannot wake a computer that is already asleep. Create a Loop When you need multiple steps, open Create Loop from the right toolbar or More tools . For full instructions, see Create Loop (multi-step flows); the shortest path is: 1. Create a Loop and add AI task, condition, HTTP request, or manual approval nodes. 2. Define the input, output, and failure handling for each node. 3. Test a single node first, then run the whole flow manually. 4. Enable schedule triggers, Webhooks, or Agent hooks only after validation. Restarting the app loses a run that was paused at a manual approval node. For important flows, save each step's input, output, and result; before rerunning, check whether a file, request, or submission has already completed, to avoid writing or submitting twice. Automation acceptance - Workspace and output paths are explicit - Runtime, model, and Skill are fixed - The shortest task has already succeeded in an ordinary session - Individual nodes and the whole flow have each passed testing - External requests, writes, and credential use have approval boundaries - Recent results, errors, and recovery methods can be found When automation fails, do not start by increasing the retry count; first open the session and node results for the most recent run and determine whether the error will repeatedly produce external effects.

en.title: Biology Room
en.description: Pin sequences, structures, genome tracks, and annotations into a traceable workspace room.
en.body: Biology Room Biology Room ships with SciForge and needs no separate plugin. It organizes the sequences, structures, genome tracks, and annotations from biological samples or experimental material into one traceable room, for viewing, annotating, and handoff. In a session, have the Agent create or open a room, then view the files in it through file preview. A room stores asset references, selections, view state, and history, and has no separate panel today. Opening it - Entry point: an Agent invokes a Biology Room capability in a session to create or open a room; files inside the room are viewed through file preview. - Applies to: biological files and room manifests in the current workspace; paths must be workspace-relative. - Prerequisite: the workspace is writable; asset extensions are supported; when an index is referenced, the index lives in the same workspace as the source file. What it can do What you want to do How to do it Output --- --- --- Create a room Give a title and optionally attach a first batch of assets Initial room manifest and revision 1 Open or create from a file Pass in one workspace file; reuse an existing room that already contains that file A new room, or the manifest of an existing room Add and manage assets Add or remove assets, or switch the current asset, against the current revision A new revision; asset fingerprint, format, modality, and readiness status Record selections and annotations Save sequence, structure, or genome selections and view state, and bind annotation anchors Structured selections, view state, and annotations stored by anchor Refresh and roll back Refresh asset fingerprints; view history and restore a revision Updated revision, orphaned annotation markers, and history events Typical workflow 1. List existing rooms first and check whether a room already contains the target file, to avoid creating duplicates. 2. Open or create a room from the file; verify the returned path, format, SHA-256, and index fingerprint. 3. Commit a set of changes against the current revision, using dry-run mode first to see whether there are changes and warnings. 4. After applying the changes, read the room again and verify the revision, asset readiness, and annotation anchors. 5. Refresh the room after source files change; to roll back, view history first, then restore the older revision to produce a new revision number. Inputs, outputs, and permissions - Read: FASTA/GenBank, PDB/mmCIF, and GFF3/BED/VCF files in the workspace, optionally with .fai , .gzi , .tbi , and .csi indexes; up to 4 indexes per asset. - Write: room manifests, revision snapshots, and event logs, stored in the room directory under .sciforge/biology/rooms/ in the workspace; source files are referenced read-only. - Approval or external effects: room writes touch workspace metadata only and do not trigger approval; put human confirmation before dry-run review, cascading asset removal, and restoring an old revision. - What it will not do: modify or delete source files, perform alignment, variant calling, or structural computation, or provide real-time multi-user collaboration; removing an asset removes only the room reference. Known limitations - Narrower support than Life Science Preview: no FASTQ, GTF, omics matrices, imaging, or spectra; gzip covers only FASTA, GFF, BED, and VCF. - A room holds at most 128 assets, 2,000 annotations, and 100 MiB of assets in total; a single unindexed asset is capped at 25 MiB. - Rooms have no standalone interface; creation, changes, and restoration all happen through the Agent in a session. - After a refresh, missing or unreadable assets are marked explicitly, and annotations that lost their anchor are marked orphaned and need human confirmation before you handle them. - Applying changes validates the revision number and rejects stale ones; history is stored by revision and may be truncated. - The collaboration boundary is sharing one room manifest and version history, not cloud-based real-time multi-user collaboration. Related pages - Life Science Preview: dedicated views for sequences, structures, and genome files in a room. - Acquiring and organizing data: download data and record its source, date, version, license, and verification results. - Workspaces and sessions: workspace location, file paths, and recovery boundaries. - Evidence & Reproducibility: fold room changes into the larger research record chain. Current version: built-in Biology Workbench 1.1.3. For what selection saving covers in the molecular preview, see Life Science Preview.

en.title: Browser Preview
en.description: Open web pages inside the app so the Agent can browse and act on pages that are visible and subject to approval.
en.body: Browser Preview Browser Preview runs a native Chromium page in the right panel for viewing local development pages, research materials, or sites that require sign-in. It is both a window for human browsing and a page resource the Agent can observe and operate. Web content is always treated as untrusted data. How to open it - Entry: Browser in the right toolbar (expand More tools if it is not shown), or Native browser in the right panel. - Target: one browser page instance in the current session; one instance corresponds to one page. - Prerequisite: the SciForge desktop window. Opening a localhost development site in an ordinary browser cannot host the native view, and an explicit unavailable message appears. - Input box context: when a message contains an HTTP(S) link, that URL is attached for the Agent. It first attempts a read-only fetch, then hands off to the browser panel when it encounters sign-in or script-rendered content. What you can do What you want to do How to do it Output --- --- --- Open a web page Enter an HTTP(S) address in the address bar and press Enter The native page, title, and current URL Browse and reload Use the Back, Forward, Reload, and Fullscreen buttons Page state and observable page content Let the Agent read Have it read the URL or current page first Bounded body text and interactive targets Let the Agent act Navigate, click, fill, or scroll under explicit instructions Page changes; actions bound to the current page version Typical workflow 1. Open Browser in the right panel and sign in to any sites you need. Sign-in state is saved in the current workspace's browser profile. 2. Have the Agent read the page first and confirm the URL, title, and key content. Do not have it click immediately. 3. When navigation is needed, you confirm it. Before clicks, key presses, or drags, check the action and its consequences. 4. Observe the page again after an action to confirm submission results, downloads, or navigation instead of relying only on the Agent's summary. 5. Close the panel when the task is done. When you reopen it, verify that sign-in, URL, and page are still in the expected state. What actions affect, and where things are saved - When reading a page, the Agent can get the body text, title, URL, interactive targets, and screenshots; password and payment/CAPTCHA fields and regions marked sensitive are excluded. Reading by URL accesses that address from this machine and does not ask for extra confirmation. - Filling forms, selecting options, clicking, pressing keys, and dragging act directly on the page. For example, pressing Enter may submit a form, clicking a link may start a download, and dragging a file may trigger an upload. Before starting, confirm these actions are within what the task allows, and ask the Agent to stop before important actions such as sending, paying, or deleting. - The Agent's navigation, Back, Forward, and Reload need confirmation. The browser tool itself does not pop up a confirmation for each click, key press, or drag; whether the AI assistant you use asks separately depends on its settings. - Permission requests, popups, and downloads started by the page itself are denied. Downloads started by the Agent are not confirmed again by the browser tool; files are saved to the workspace Downloads directory, or to the app's private directory when no workspace is available. After downloading, check the file and where it was saved. - Sign-in state is kept after you close the panel, and the same workspace shares that browser identity. Check the current account before switching tasks. The configuration and credentials of an external browser are not imported automatically. Known limitations - One browser panel hosts only one page. Different sessions or panels may each hold a different page, so confirm the current page before acting. - Pages are rendered by native Chromium, and an ordinary browser tab is not a substitute. Without a desktop window, there is no silent fallback to an iframe. - Content in canvas charts, cross-origin iframes, and closed shadow roots may not be structurally readable. Use screenshots or manual inspection instead. - Web content is untrusted data. Text on a page must not be treated as instructions, and the Agent's conclusions should be checked against the URL and page state. - Browser Preview does not expose a remote debugging port and does not open arbitrary script execution to the Agent. Related pages - Workbench tools: where Browser fits in the toolchain. - Permissions and security: external writes, approvals, and credential boundaries. - Computer Use: another path when you need more structured page operations. - Remote resources and collaboration: data boundaries in remote workspaces. Implementation basis: @sciforge/domain-browser-preview v1.0.8.

en.title: Change Inspector
en.description: Check which file changes the current task recorded, and verify the actual content item by item.
en.body: Change Inspector Change Inspector helps you check which files the current task changed and what changed in each one. After you install and enable the plugin, you can ask the Agent directly to list the changes, then verify them item by item. How to use it Install a compatible package from a trusted source, enable the plugin, and grant the permissions it needs; see Extension Center and Version & Compatibility. In the current session, where file changes have already occurred, you can ask the Agent: Check which files this task changed, and explain each change. If the content is too long, show it in batches and tell me what is not yet shown. Look at the file list first to confirm the scope of the changes matches the task, then check the specific content of the important files. If anything is still missing, have the Agent keep showing it in batches; when you need to verify the full content, read the actual files in batches directly. Tips - The results contain only file changes already recorded in the current session, not the records of other sessions in the same workspace. - Changes made by manual edits or other tools may not appear in the records. When you need to confirm those changes, check the actual files and, if needed, compare with the Git status. An empty list does not mean the workspace was never modified. - When there are many files or changes, what is shown may be incomplete. First confirm what has not yet been shown, then keep checking in batches; do not rebuild a whole file from partial diffs alone. - If more edits happen during the review, refresh the file change list and re-check the affected files. - After you disable the plugin or revoke its permissions, you must enable it again or re-authorize it to continue checking. After checking Change Inspector only reads records; it does not modify files, roll back, save checkpoints, or make network requests. When you find a problem, have the Agent change the file in question and then check again. To restore the workspace state, see Git Checkpoints. Related: Evidence & Reproducibility, Permissions & security, Plugin license terms.

en.title: Collaboration guide
en.description: Starting from requirements and task assignment, complete member acceptance, human review, delivery adoption, and project close-out.
en.body: Collaboration guide The owner writes clear requirements and confirms the division of work. Members accept tasks, execute them in their own SciForge, review drafts, and submit. Finally the owner adopts the result. Tasks that hand off to one another use the files already adopted upstream. Open a collaboration project 1. Expand the left sidebar and complete cloud sign-in and device connection in the account area at the bottom. 2. In the sidebar's collaboration area, open a project, My work , or Inbox . If you cannot see the project tree, expand the sidebar first. 3. In an ordinary session, confirm the Runtime and model respond before starting a collaboration task. Each member uses their own cloud account. Project requirements, discussions, result notes, and submitted files go to the collaboration service; an ordinary local workspace is not synced as a whole directory. Do not put model keys or sign-in credentials into any of these. Once a project is selected, there are five tabs at the top: Tab Purpose --- --- Board See tasks and the progress of acceptance, assignment, review, and adoption Members See project members; invite or manage members according to your current role Requirements Edit goals, inputs, work modules, and acceptance criteria, and confirm requirements Shared files See shared material, sealed task deliveries, and project results Project info See the project description, status, and available management actions 1. The owner prepares and confirms requirements 1. In the collaboration project area, use + to create a project and fill in a name. 2. Open Requirements and edit Goals & deliverables and Inputs & boundaries . State the data sources, final files, how acceptance works, and the actions that must not be performed. 3. Click Save requirements and wait for the work modules to be completed. On failure, read the message, check the model configuration, then use Regenerate . 4. Check each module's goal, inputs, outputs, dependencies, and acceptance criteria. When all are correct, click Confirm requirements . 5. Invite members under Members . Invitees enter from the inbox or the project invitation prompt, read the requirements, and accept the invitation. For example: "B counts the total samples and submits a report; C continues the comparison using the report B had adopted. The report must include the method, validation results, and limitations." Also provide inputs the members can actually read. Dependencies between tasks. 2. Check assignments and blocking reasons On the board, the owner opens a task and checks the executor and upstream dependencies. Depending on the task's current state, choose a member and Assign task or Reassign , or Change assignee or Withdraw assignment for an assignment not yet accepted. A module with dependencies waits until its upstream result is adopted. The interface keeps the assign entry and shows the reason, with the button disabled. Finish the upstream review first. If a task is still unassigned after requirements are confirmed, or assignment failed and no member is available, the owner needs to pick an executor or handle the to-do as prompted. Do not treat a task waiting to be assigned as already running. 3. Members decide whether to accept Members can see incoming assignments from Inbox, My work, a board task card, or task details . Read the goal, file requirements, dependencies, and validity period first, then choose: Action Result --- --- Accept task Confirms you take the task; it runs once your local Runtime is ready, or you are prompted to recover it Ignore Handles the current assignment, and the task is removed from your related lists; it is not the same as dismissing a notice bar Decline Explicitly declines the current assignment; the owner rearranges it according to the project state Go by the buttons actually available; an assignment that has expired or been handled cannot be accepted again. Dismissing the assignment reminder on the board does not perform "Ignore" for you. After accepting, use the task session to see run progress and tool calls. 4. Handle agent questions and action confirmations When a task needs more information, the designated member answers in the task details. If a request involves actions such as modifying files, writing to external systems, or deleting, first read the specific action, its scope of impact, the request version, and its validity period, write a decision note, then click Approve this action or Decline this action . Only the designated member can decide, and an expired request must wait to be refreshed. After submitting a decision, check the confirmation and later task progress; whether the action completed depends on what actually ran. An ordinary discussion message does not replace action approval. 5. Members review the draft and submit 1. When execution finishes, open the delivery draft, preview the required files, and check the content. 2. Edit the Result note , stating what was actually done, the check results, and limitations. 3. To add material, click Add material : choose this run's output from Task files , or use Upload from this computer . Extra material does not replace the required files. 4. To have the AI revise, go to the task session through Ask AI to revise . 5. Check the file list and click Submit . In the confirmation window, check the version, note, and files, then confirm the submission. While submitting, wait for a clear result from device verification, signing, and file upload. If a system secure-storage authorization prompt appears, handle it yourself. On success, a versioned delivery snapshot is created and waits for the owner's review. This version cannot be edited in place; a revision creates a new version. One delivery can hold at most 20 files, no more than 200 MiB in total; each attached file is at most 100 MiB. Required files may also have task-specific format and size requirements, so follow the submission window's prompts. The result note, required files, and extra material in a delivery draft. Delivery files uploading and the submission progress. 6. The owner reviews and hands off downstream On the board, open a task pending confirmation, preview this version's files, and read the result note against the acceptance criteria. To ask for more, use Request revision and write specific feedback; the member revises, rechecks, and submits a new version. When the requirements are met, click Adopt , and the task moves to Completed. History keeps older snapshots, so check the current version when reviewing. Only after the upstream is adopted can a downstream task continue to assignment; downstream execution uses the files of the adopted version. The owner writing revision requirements. Delivery version history. 7. View shared files and close out Shared files lists project files by source and version, and lets you preview submitted content. Upload file here is currently unavailable and shows the reason. To submit material with a task, go back to Add material in the delivery draft; do not wait for an upload to succeed on the Shared files page. After all modules are adopted, the owner checks the results and limitations, then uses the Close project entry to confirm completion and waits for signing and the server result. After all tasks are adopted, the owner confirms close-out. Board status at a glance Column Meaning Next step --- --- --- Inbox The module has not been assigned, perhaps waiting on a dependency or manual assignment The owner checks the blocking reason and executor To start Assigned, waiting for the member to accept The member reads, then accepts, ignores, or declines In progress Running, waiting for a human answer, or the member is reviewing the draft Check task details and handle the current request Pending confirmation A delivery has been submitted The owner reviews, requests revision, or adopts Completed The module's result is adopted The owner closes the project once all modules are done On a network interruption, submission failure, or signature error, keep the draft first, check sign-in and device status, and after recovery check whether a submission record already exists before retrying as prompted. Continue reading: Pasilla three-person collaboration case, Identity & Access, Runtime & models.

en.title: Computer Use
en.description: Enable Computer Use so Codex or Claude Code can operate browser and in-app embedded pages within the scope you authorize.
en.body: Computer Use Computer Use lets the Agent observe a page and click, type, press keys, or scroll step by step, which suits tasks that must be done through an interface. It currently supports Codex and Claude Code only , and its scope is browser pages and the embedded pages of Electron apps, such as Browser Preview; it cannot be used to operate arbitrary desktop applications. Enable and check 1. Open Settings → AI assistant → Computer use , turn on the main switch, and choose Codex or Claude Code for this use. 2. Check the run status on the settings page; if it is unavailable, handle the page's prompt first. 3. In macOS System Settings, grant the Screen Recording and Accessibility permissions, then return to the app and confirm the status. 4. Open the target page, and in the session state the task, the allowed actions, the stopping conditions, and the forbidden actions. Figure 1: Enable Computer Use on the settings page, and check its run status and system permissions. Run a task 1. First have the Agent observe the current page, and check the page identity and the target content. 2. Carry out actions step by step. Every call that changes state needs your confirmation; check the specific action before allowing it, because a confirmation does not authorize later actions of the same kind. 3. Before signing in, authorizing, sending, uploading, buying, paying, deleting, or submitting a formal result, confirm the target of the action and its consequences. 4. When done, stop the task or release the session, and go back to the page to check the actual result. What actions affect, and tips - Observation reads the page content, interactive elements, and screenshots; read-only queries need no confirmation. - Clicking, typing, key presses, and scrolling act directly on the target page and may submit something or change the page state. - Pages and screenshots may contain accounts, patient information, or unpublished data; check and redact before sharing or exporting. Do not have the Agent fill in passwords, verification codes, or payment information. - When the run status is unavailable or system permissions are insufficient, fix the problem before continuing the task. - When the session ends, the current operating connection is released. Computer Use is not suited to unattended, long-running automation. Related pages - Permissions & security: system permissions and confirmation of key actions. - Skills, MCP, and Extensions: tool connections and extension management. - Browser Preview: the main page entry that can currently be operated. - Workbench tools: how the tools divide the work, and usage principles. Implementation basis: @sciforge/domain-computer-use v1.0.1.

en.title: Content Space
en.description: View the connected note service and choose an open notebook in SiYuan.
en.body: Content Space Content Space is for viewing the connected note service and choosing a notebook. It currently supports SiYuan Notes, and lists only notebooks that are open and not closed in SiYuan. The note content stays in the original SiYuan service. Open it and choose a notebook 1. First connect your own SiYuan service as described on the SiYuan Notes page. 2. Open Content Space in the right panel; Shared files on the full Collaboration page also provides this entry. 3. Choose the connected SiYuan service, then choose a notebook from the list. If you cannot find the one you want, first confirm in SiYuan that the notebook is open. 4. To read, edit, or search documents, open the SiYuan Notes page, or have the Agent use SiYuan's search, read, and write tools. Tips - Content Space currently offers notebook selection only; you cannot browse or edit SiYuan documents, or upload or download files, here. - The Shared files entry also has no direct upload button for now. Choosing a notebook does not send local files into SiYuan. - When the connection is no longer valid, first check the SiYuan service address and connection status, then reconnect. - Document edits and Agent writes affect the connected SiYuan service; before acting, confirm the target notebook and document. Related pages - SiYuan Notes: connect the service, edit and search, and archive tasks. - Collaboration: how Shared files relates to task delivery files. - Permissions & security: external writes and confirmation rules. - Feature status and limitations: the current status of each capability. Implementation basis: @sciforge/domain-content-space v5.0.4.

en.title: Create Loop (multi-step workflows)
en.description: Chain AI, conditions, HTTP, and human approvals in multi-node workflows.
en.body: Create Loop (multi-step workflows) Create Loop breaks a task into multiple inspectable steps. It sits above session execution: AI nodes generate or decide, condition and data-processing nodes control the path, HTTP nodes connect external systems, subflows reuse another Loop, and human approvals determine whether key actions proceed. Before using it, confirm that the models, network, and tools the chosen nodes need are available, and run the whole flow through in your current environment. How to open it - Entry: Create Loop in the right toolbar (expand More tools if it is not shown). Edit nodes on the canvas; the right panel shows settings for the current Loop. - Target: one Loop in the current workspace. Definitions and run records are stored on this machine. - Prerequisite: AI nodes need an available Runtime and model, HTTP nodes need network access, and schedules and local webhooks are triggered by the app process, so the app must remain running. A Loop can be started with manual Run once , a schedule, a webhook, or an Agent hook. What you can do What you want to do How to do it Output --- --- --- Chain a multi-step task Add AI agent task , LLM generation , Condition , HTTP request , human approval, subflow, and other nodes from the left node panel, then connect them A Loop you can save Branch on data Organize inputs and outputs with Condition, Switch, Merge, Filter, Loop, and similar nodes Explicit data flow between nodes Validate before going live Use Test node with mock upstream input for a single node, then Run once for the whole Loop Node results and run logs Stop at key points Add a Human Approval node, set the title, instruction, and timeout, then Approve/Reject on the card or in the run drawer Controlled release Trigger automatically Configure a schedule, webhook, or Agent hook Scheduled, external, or event-driven triggers Typical workflow 1. Open Create Loop from the right toolbar or More tools , name it, and confirm the working directory. AI, image, and code nodes all use that directory. 2. Add trigger and task nodes and connect them in execution order. Write clear input references, error handling, and timeouts for each node. 3. Use Test node with mock upstream input to validate a single node first. The current Loop is saved before testing. 4. Click Run once and check each node's input, output, timing, and errors in the Run log , Run history , and Audit report . 5. After validation, turn on Enabled , enable AI-callable as needed, configure schedules or webhooks, and keep human approvals before key steps. Figure 1: The Create Loop canvas connects multiple processing nodes into a runnable flow. Select a node to inspect its parameters on the right. Where things are saved, and what actions affect - Loop definitions and run history are saved on this machine. The run log and audit report show each step's input, output, and result; for important flows, also save the results you need to keep to an agreed location. - Nodes may read or write workspace files, and may use the output of upstream nodes. Before running, check the working directory and output paths; before a rerun, check existing files and submissions that already completed, to avoid repeating operations. - Starting a whole flow, stopping a run, and handling approvals all need confirmation. HTTP and AI nodes send real requests and may incur costs; Test node also performs real operations. - Raw Secret values are not written to run records. Manual approval needs you to choose approve or reject; after the app restarts, a run paused at that point cannot be resumed. Known limitations - Restarting the app loses a run that was paused at a manual approval. Before rerunning, look at the inputs, outputs, and results each step saved, and confirm which operations have already completed, to avoid writing or submitting twice. - Schedules and webhooks depend on the app process. They do not fire while the app is closed. - A step that needs a Secret must be able to obtain the credentials it needs when rerun; if they are unavailable, execution stops, and you must restore the configuration first. - A single-node test proves only that node, not the whole flow. Tests also execute the node logic for real. - When randomness is not fixed, rerun differences are marked as indeterminate and cannot be treated directly as a reproduction failure. Related pages - Automation and scheduled tasks: scheduled execution of a single AI instruction, and when to use Create Loop instead. - Evidence & Reproducibility: run records, artifact versions, and the evidence chain. - Agent workflows: Agent hooks and execution boundaries in sessions. - Permissions and security: external requests, writes, and confirmation rules. Implementation basis: @sciforge/domain-create-loop v1.1.4.

en.title: Acquiring and organizing data
en.description: Obtain data with the provider's client or your own scripts, and keep records of source, version, license, and verification.
en.body: Acquiring and organizing data Use a client the data provider supports, or run a download script in an environment you have configured. First confirm access rights, terms of use, and the storage space you need; manage credentials as described in Permissions & security. 1. Confirm the data source URL, the data version, and the license, and record the access or download date. 2. Download with the provider's client or a script, and keep the commands, download parameters, and results actually used. 3. Check the file size and SHA-256; when the provider publishes checksums, compare against them one by one and record the verification result. 4. When organizing files, keep the original data. Save cleaning, filtering, or format conversions as separate results, and record how inputs, processing scripts, and outputs correspond. Supported downloaded files can be viewed in Life Science Preview, and Biology Room can organize the sequence, structure, and genome assets it supports. Previewing and organizing assets do not replace downloading, integrity checks, or analysis. Data acquisition, cleaning, and scientific conclusions each need real execution and source records; see Evidence & reproducibility.

en.title: Evidence & Reproducibility
en.description: Use artifact versions, checkpoints, Evidence DAG, and Research Dossier to pin down the research process and results.
en.body: Evidence & Reproducibility SciForge keeps a research task's inputs, process, and results through artifact versions, run records, and source links, so you can recheck them and continue the research. Choose a recording method as you need. Artifact versions, checkpoints, the evidence graph, and the research dossier use built-in entry points in the app; Change Inspector needs a plugin installed and enabled. For version requirements, see Version & Compatibility. Recording feature Purpose and how it is provided --- --- Artifact Versions Save independent versions of a single artifact; compare and restore earlier results Git Checkpoints Automatically save the Git workspace state at the start and end of a task Research Checkpoints Automatically save the research summary, sources, and file references of completed turns Change Inspector Use a plugin to check the file changes already recorded in the current session Evidence DAG Save and check the conclusions and evidence relationships in the current session Project DAG Manually combine the evidence graphs each session has saved, to check project progress Research Dossier Read a selected research record, check versions and limitations, and prepare delivery Choose the right record object Object Problem it solves Typical content --- --- --- Session How did the task progress? Messages, tool calls, commands, approvals, and the final response Artifact Version How did a figure or file evolve? Artifact path, version, inputs, and generation details Git Checkpoint What stage are the workspace files at? Git status and stage-level code snapshots Research Checkpoint How do I continue a research stage? Research context, key artifacts, and resume location Evidence DAG What supports or refutes a claim? Claims, sources, methods, artifacts, limitations, and relationships Research Dossier How does someone else read the final deliverable? Research question, inputs, methods, results, credibility, and limitations Build a checkable chain Recommended order: 1. At the start of the task, record the workspace, input versions, and objective; a Git workspace automatically saves a checkpoint from before the task started. 2. After the analysis, save the actual sources, commands, parameters, result files, and figures, and save independent versions of the artifacts you want to keep. 3. Wait for this round's research record to be saved, then open the research dossier to check the summary, references, and selected versions. Confirm the summary record and the actual files separately. 4. In Evidence DAG, click Update , wait for the evidence graph to finish saving, then check item by item the relationship between conclusions and sources, counter-evidence, and missing information. 5. When you need a cross-session summary, first confirm each session's evidence graph is saved, then click Update now in Project DAG; after it finishes, review the current project graph. 6. In the research dossier, check the selected record and its limitations, and before delivery verify the related files, versions, and sharing permissions. Figure 1: The research dossier shows the research narrative, selected versions, a credibility summary, and the limitations that need attention together. Have the Agent leave a complete record You can add this to a task: After the analysis, organize the research question, input files, methods used, key parameters, results, and limitations into the research dossier. Every key conclusion should trace back to its source, derived table, or figure; mark anything you cannot confirm as unverified. Do not only ask it to "generate an Evidence DAG". First make clear which claims deserve review, which data can directly support them, and which explanations are still candidate hypotheses. Manual review checklist - Can every key number be traced back to the input files and the computation steps? - Do the figures come from verified derived tables, not intermediate files edited by hand? - Does the conclusion confuse correlation, prediction, and causation? - Are counter-evidence, warnings, and missing data still visible? - Are the code commit, environment, parameters, and random seed needed for a rerun complete? - Does each checkpoint correspond to a Git state you have already checked? Before you rely on it A standalone plugin must be installed and enabled first. For installation requirements, see the plugin list. For the evidence graph, use the built-in entry point in the app. The optional standalone Evidence DAG plugin cannot yet be used fully in the app; for the availability and licenses of optional plugins, see the plugin list. Scientific Figures saves its own code, inputs, environment, runs, and image history, and does not register them with Artifact Versions or Evidence DAG automatically. When you include a figure in a deliverable, link the actual inputs, runs, and outputs explicitly, and recheck them before forming a claim. Data boundary Evidence DAG and Research Dossier show meaningful content only when the current workspace and session already have the matching data. An empty panel does not mean the feature is broken; first have the task produce clear claims, sources, and artifact records. Case: ECCITE-seq cross-scale virtual cell evidence graph.

en.title: Evidence DAG
en.description: Connect claims in a session to their sources, methods, artifacts, and limitations.
en.body: Evidence DAG Evidence DAG helps you check what a conclusion rests on: in the graph, see the sources, computation steps, figures, and limitations that support or refute it. First finish the analysis and save the sources, results, and related files, then click Update to save the evidence graph; after the update finishes, separately check the relationships and gaps in the graph. To combine several sessions, use Project DAG. Opening it - Entry: in the Research panel, click View evidence graph . When the standalone evidence panel is open, switch from the default Research record to Evidence graph . - Target: the evidence graph already saved in the current session. - Prerequisite: the task has left sources, an analysis process, and result records, and the evidence-graph feature and the text-reasoning configuration are available. Save and check the evidence graph 1. Finish a round of analysis, and save the sources actually used, the computation records, the result files, and the matching artifact versions; make clear which are conclusions and which are still hypotheses. 2. Click Update , wait for queueing and execution to finish, and confirm the new evidence graph has been saved. Updating calls the configured text-reasoning service and saves evidence records, with no extra approval. 3. In the graph, select a conclusion and its related nodes, and check item by item whether the sources, runs, code, environment, and artifact versions support it. Even after a successful save, this review is still yours to do. 4. Check whether the conclusion can be traced to its sources, find missing records and known limitations, and handle the prompts about a missing source, an unverified version, or a missing approval. After adding real records, update again and check the result. 5. To combine several sessions, first confirm this session's evidence graph has been saved, then go to Project DAG and update the project graph manually. Further checks - Click Audit to check the structure of the saved evidence graph and see the gap hints. For now it only checks the graph's structure (L0); you still have to judge whether a conclusion has a scientific basis. - Select a Conclusion node and click Download rerun spec to download the configuration notes needed to rerun the analysis. Before rerunning, also confirm that the input files, software, parameters, environment, and related result files are available; downloading the spec does not run the analysis. - To check whether an analysis can be rerun under its original conditions, verify that the input files, software versions, parameters, environment, run records, logs, and result files are complete and verifiable. If the analysis involves randomness, also record the random seed; this is also required to reach the L4 reproducibility level. Tips - If no claims, sources, or artifacts have been saved yet, the graph may be empty. Save the analysis records and actual files first, then update the evidence graph. - If an update fails, you can keep viewing the graph saved before, but make sure you know which result you are reviewing. Only a saved graph can be used for audit. - When a source or run record is missing, the graph shows a prompt. Go back to the actual source and run records to check; a chat summary alone cannot fill the gap. - Restricted evidence may not be previewable, and you should respect the source's access permissions. - Rebuilding is only for upgrades, corruption recovery, or reinterpretation, and needs a stated reason and justification; for everyday additions to the record, use Update. Related pages - Evidence & Reproducibility: the group overview and the recommended record chain. - Project DAG: combine the evidence graphs several sessions have saved into a project view. - Research Dossier: read research records and prepare delivery. - Artifact Versions: save the artifact versions that evidence references. - Virtual cell evidence atlas case: how evidence is organized in a complete task.

en.title: Skills, MCP, and Extensions
en.description: See where capabilities come from in the Extension Center, manage extensions and Skills, and check MCP and desktop-control permissions.
en.body: Skills, MCP, and Extensions When you need to add tools or a specialized method, first work out what you are installing, then check its source and permissions. Extensions provide app panels and tools, Skills provide task methods, and MCP connects external tools or data. Open the Extension Center Open Extensions from the left sidebar to see built-in and installed extensions, the marketplace, and Skills. Expand the sidebar first if you need the full navigation. Extension details show the publisher, version, source, status, permissions, and the features it contributes. After installing or enabling, related entries may appear in the left navigation, the vertical toolbar on the far right, or file preview. When there are many toolbar entries, use More tools ; supported entries can be adjusted through Customize toolbar . For understanding extension sources and feature details. Install and manage extensions In the marketplace, pick an entry and read the description, publisher, permissions, and installation status before confirming the install. Whether it can be installed depends on the current index and app compatibility; a blocked entry shows the reason. Ordinary local installation uses an official signed package, and checks the signature, file contents, and compatibility with the app version. Development sources are labeled separately and must not be treated as official signed installs. Files in a workspace never become enabled extensions automatically. Installed extensions can be enabled, disabled, uninstalled, or rolled back with the operations the interface offers; built-in extensions are managed with the app version. If it says a restart is needed, or the extension is invalid or failed to load, handle that prompt first, then check the feature's entry point. Extension pages that support docking can be placed on the left, right, bottom, or in the main area, and used together with the session. Changing position does not widen the extension's permissions. Use a Skill A Skill usually contains method notes plus supporting scripts and material. Before enabling it, check: - What tasks it suits, and when it triggers. - Whether it runs scripts, accesses the network, or writes files. - What software, data, and credentials it needs. - What check shows the result is reliable. Shows what project-level and global Skill management is for. Once a Skill is discovered, its scripts still run under the task's permissions. Dependency installs and external actions of a third-party Skill need separate checks; "enabled" is not a substitute for authorization. Connect an MCP Server When configuring MCP, check the service source, version, launch method or address, the credential scope, and what data the tools will read or send. Test the connection with low-impact operations first, then move to tasks that write. Before sending, uploading, deleting, or modifying anything in an external system, confirm the target and the user's authorization. A successful connection only shows that the service can be called; the task result still needs checking. Avoid writing keys directly into prompts, project requirements, or delivery content. Use Computer Use Computer Use currently supports Codex and Claude Code, and can operate browsers and the embedded pages of Electron apps. First enable it in settings and check the run status; on macOS, also check the Screen Recording and Accessibility permissions. Limit the target page and the task scope, and check each action such as sign-in, authorization, payment, sending, or deleting. After enabling Computer Use, check the run status and system permissions. When you cannot find a feature 1. Check the status and error messages of the extension, Skill, or MCP. 2. Check whether the current workspace, permissions, and Runtime support the capability you need. 3. Start a new session so capabilities are discovered again; if a restart is needed, follow the interface prompt. 4. If a tool entry has disappeared, check More tools and the toolbar customization settings. 5. If a local extension fails to install, check the publisher, signature, and version compatibility; do not force-load it by turning off permission checks. Related pages: Workbench tools, Permissions & security.

en.title: Git Checkpoints
en.description: Automatically save Git checkpoints at the start and end of a task, and leave a rescue snapshot before restoring.
en.body: Git Checkpoints Git Checkpoints automatically saves the workspace's Git state at the start and end of a task turn, so you can check what this turn changed and, when needed, restore an earlier state. For the research summary, sources, and where to continue the research, see Research Checkpoints. Opening it - Entry: Git Checkpoints in the right toolbar (expand More tools if it is not shown); the right panel is titled Git Checkpoints as well. - Target: the local Git workspace bound to the current session. - Prerequisite: the workspace is a Git repository and Git features are available; a non-Git workspace produces no checkpoints. View and restore 1. Start a task in a Git workspace, and the system automatically saves a checkpoint from before the start; you do not need to save one by hand or keep the panel open. 2. After the task turn finishes or ends, open the panel or click the refresh icon, and check the records from before the start and after the end. 3. Select a checkpoint, read the file differences and the change summary, and confirm it matches the state you want to restore. 4. When you need to restore, click Restore and confirm. The system first saves a rescue checkpoint; if saving fails, the restore is aborted. 5. After restoring, check the actual workspace files and the Git status. To see the file changes the current task recorded, you can use Change Inspector. Confirm before restoring Restoring rewrites workspace files, so first confirm the target checkpoint, and check whether there are changes you still need to keep. The rescue checkpoint saves the state from before the restore, so you can get back the work that this restore overwrote. The panel offers a list, a diff preview, refresh, and restore, with no button to create a checkpoint by hand. The diff preview may show only part of the content; when a preview is incomplete, check the actual files and the Git diff further before restoring. What is saved A Git checkpoint saves the workspace's Git state, which suits reviewing code and file changes. The research question, sources, and next-step plan still need to be recorded through research checkpoints; versions of a single figure or data file can be saved separately as Artifact Versions. Related pages - Evidence & Reproducibility: the group overview and the recommended record chain. - Research Checkpoints: save research context and the resume location. - Artifact Versions: save versions of a single artifact. - Change Inspector: check which file changes a session recorded. - Workspaces and sessions: how the workspace, sessions, and Git state relate.

en.title: Identity & Access
en.description: Manage the local account, cloud sign-in, device connection, and usage summary from the bottom of the sidebar.
en.body: Identity & Access Expand the workbench's left sidebar and look at the bottom for the local account, cloud status, and usage summary . Click the account row to open the account panel; click the cloud row to open the same panel positioned at SciForge Cloud . Settings sits below it. A local account is an attribution marker Local features do not require sign-in. You can create a local account, confirm its display name, choose an account or rename it, and sign out of the account. A local account provides no security authentication and does not isolate workspaces, chats, settings, API keys, or tool data . On a shared computer, switching the display name is no substitute for operating-system account isolation. The delete button on an account row first shows a confirmation area. Once confirmed, it deletes that local account and its attribution data on this machine, and this cannot be undone. When you delete the current account, the system selects the earliest-created remaining account; after the last account is deleted, no account is selected. Delete account here is local identity management. It is not cloud account cancellation, project deletion, or workspace file cleanup.
