Signing out of a local account, signing out of the cloud, and disconnecting a device each do something different, so check the button name and its target before acting. Sign in to the cloud and connect a device 1. Create or choose a local account first. Until one is selected, "Browser sign-in" is unavailable. 2. Under SciForge Cloud , click Browser sign-in and complete authentication in the system browser. You do not need to paste a password or token into a session. 3. After returning, check the cloud identity. If no device is connected yet, click Connect this device . 4. Collaboration features that depend on cloud identity can continue only when the identity is valid and the device is active. The local account, the model provider sign-in, and the SciForge cloud sign-in are separate configurations. Cloud features depend on the current app configuration and service availability. Panel state or action Meaning and what to do --- --- Not signed in to the cloud Local features still work; cloud projects need sign-in This device is not connected Being signed in is not a device connection; connect the device from the interface Connecting this device Wait for the device registration result and avoid repeating the action This device is connected The device is active; a valid cloud identity and project permission are still required This device is disconnected / connection error Cloud permissions cannot be used as if connected normally; check the error and recover as prompted Sign in again Completes cloud authentication again; it does not automatically accept project invitations or tasks Sign out Clears the current cloud sign-in session; do not treat it as having revoked the device registration Disconnect this device Revokes this device's cloud access; local features are kept When a device is revoked, the identity changes, or device validity cannot be confirmed, cloud authentication rights are withdrawn. Do not use a cached display name to decide you are still authorized. If sign-in or connection fails, retry as the panel suggests and keep the original task and drafts. Reading the usage summary The bottom of the sidebar shows token and cost summaries for today and the last 7 days recorded on this machine; for the actual charges, check the model provider's bill. Loading, no data, and load failure each show their own message. No data does not mean no model requests were made. Credentials and recovery boundaries Cloud sign-in material and device keys are managed by the platform's secure storage. When secure storage is unavailable, do not fall back to plaintext files or put credentials into chats, requirements, or delivery files. When the local identity database is unavailable, other local features still work. The recovery entry asks you to type a confirmation text, first creates and verifies a backup, and then resets the local identity data. It is not a reset tool for the whole app's data. Related pages: Collaboration, Runtime & models, Permissions & security.

en.title: Life Science Preview
en.description: View structure, sequence, omics, imaging, and spectral files directly in the workspace.
en.body: Life Science Preview Life Science Preview ships with SciForge and lets you open scientific files such as sequences and molecular structures directly, with no separate plugin needed. Opening it - Entry point: file preview in the file panel; open a supported local or remote workspace file. - Applies to: workspace files. The view is chosen from the extension and the preview manifest. - Prerequisite: the file is in the current workspace. For a file in a remote workspace, it is read from the remote side, and previewing does not require downloading the whole file to this machine first. What it can do What you want to do How Output --- --- --- View molecular structures Open .pdb , .cif , .mmcif , .sdf , .mol , .mol2 , .xyz Chain, residue, and ligand summary; Mol view; distance, angle, or dihedral measurement when coordinates are available View sequences and genomes Open .fasta , .fa , .fna , .faa , .fastq , .gb , .gbk , .gff , .gff3 , .gtf , .bed , .vcf Record count, length, features, intervals, variant summary, and region selection View omics matrices Open .h5ad , .loom , .mtx , .h5 , .hdf5 , .zarr Matrix dimensions, observation/variable keys, embedding names, and a metadata summary View biological imaging Open .tif , .tiff , .ome.tif , .ome.tiff , .czi , .svs , .ndpi Size, channels, OME metadata, region of interest (ROI) and channel selection; thumbnails and tiles for TIFF/OME-TIFF View spectra and proteomics Open .mzml , .mzxml , .mgf , .fcs Scan/event summary, peak count, intensity range, sampled peaks, and peak-interval annotations Carry a companion index Open .fai , .gzi , .tbi , .csi Transported as the companion index of a sequence or genome file, for later object references What is not parsed: For omics, only metadata is read; HDF5, AnnData, Loom, and Zarr matrices are not decoded. CZI, SVS, and NDPI give only container-metadata placeholders and no pixel decoding. FCS mainly shows the visible header, keywords, and a sampled-peak summary, without a full event matrix. Trajectory and density files can be handed to the Mol view, but they are outside the scope of chain, residue, and ligand summaries. The preview is a reading aid, not validation-grade format parsing or an analysis tool. Molecular selection and what gets saved In the selection panel of the molecular preview, choose a chain or ligand, and the 3D view highlights the matching part; click Clear to remove the highlight. A selection can include multiple chains, residues, atoms, or ligands, and selecting does not modify the source file. After changing a selection, reopen the file and confirm the selection was saved. Check especially when you make several selections in quick succession; before reopening, do not judge from the current highlight alone that the selection has been saved. Typical workflow 1. Confirm the workspace location at the top, and open the target file in the file panel. 2. Check the format, size, dimensions, or record count in the preview to make sure you opened the right file. 3. To continue the analysis, create a region, residue, or channel selection and let the agent work on the original file. 4. In a remote workspace, first confirm that reading happens on the remote side. Do not have the agent copy a whole large file just for the preview. 5. Treat preview results only as session context. Key conclusions should still go back to the original file and the computation records. What previewing and exporting affect - A preview summary reads only the beginning of the file, up to 2,000,000 bytes of text and 4 MiB of binary. Anything beyond that is marked as truncated, and the summary must not be treated as complete data. - Previewing does not modify the source file. Exporting copies the source file, in the same format, to a new workspace path, which suits keeping a copy. - Opening and reading need no confirmation; exporting a copy needs confirmation, so check the target path before running it. - Previewing and exporting do not convert formats, repair damaged files, or upload workspace files; when you need those, arrange a separate task. Known limitations - Observation lists are truncated with an explicit marker, and selections that are too large are rejected. - Omics matrices, proprietary imaging containers, and FCS get metadata or placeholder previews only, so do not use them for quantitative analysis. - Thumbnails and tiles for biological imaging are attempted only for TIFF/OME-TIFF; compressed or non-8-bit TIFFs may fall back to metadata. - Sequence and genome previews are based on truncated text and cannot replace full format validation or variant calling. - Unregistered extensions do not enter the dedicated views above and are still handled as ordinary workspace files. Related pages - Biology Room: organize multiple sequences, structures, and annotations into a traceable room. - Acquiring and organizing data: download data and record its source, date, version, license, and verification results. - Workbench tools: how files, the terminal, the browser, and other entry points divide the work. - Feature status & limits: see the current position on each capability. Current version: built-in Biology Workbench 1.1.3. Preview reads and file transfer are still subject to workspace permissions and size limits.

en.title: Features & Extensions overview
en.description: Choose workbench, research analysis, evidence, collaboration, and extension capabilities by the task you want to do.
en.body: Features & Extensions overview Pick the task you want to do from the table below. Built-in features open directly; standalone plugins must be installed; Skills provide working methods; MCP connects external tools. For version information, see Version & Compatibility. Start from your task What you want to do Where to read Current form and conditions --- --- --- Open a project, continue a session, view or edit files Workbench Local workspace, sessions, and file preview for supported formats. When content is too long or a file does not support editing, the page shows the reason. Connect models and executors Runtime & models Codex, Claude Code, and DSH are configured separately. Model access and tool permissions are not the same thing. View sequences, structures, omics, imaging, and spectra Life Science Preview Ships with the app; no separate install needed. Organize biological objects and experiment records Biology Room Ships with the app; used to organize related files and annotations. Plot from data and code, revise, and accept candidates Scientific Figures Needs a compatible plugin installed, plus Python and the required dependencies. Add anchored comments to text or resources Anchored Comments Standalone plugin. Real capture and external feedback each have their own permission requirements. Check what the agent actually changed Change Inspector Plugin you must install. Lets the agent list this session's file differences, and tells you when output is too long. Save artifacts and research evidence Evidence & reproducibility Saves file versions, research stages, and the source of conclusions. Figure records must be linked separately. Run repeated tasks Automation, Create Loop Needs the app running and the matching executor. Multi-step flows and single scheduled instructions are configured separately. Sign in, connect a device, join a project, and deliver tasks Account, Collaboration Local accounts and cloud identity are separate. Team actions also need an available service and role authorization. Use Content Space and notes Content Space, SiYuan Notes You configure the matching service. Server deployment tutorials are not included. Add plugins, working methods, or external tools Extensions & marketplace Compatible signed packages, Skills, and MCP are each configured separately. An empty marketplace does not mean built-in features were uninstalled. Evidence and tool reference - Artifact Versions, Git Checkpoints, Research Checkpoints: fix the state of files or research stages. - Evidence DAG, Project DAG, Research Dossier: organize evidence, project goals, and deliverables. - Terminal, Browser Preview, Computer Use: use external execution capabilities according to the runtime environment and permissions. - Plugin license terms: check licenses and installation requirements. Remote SSH connection and management belong to internal supplements, and the public manual does not provide VPN, SSH target registration, or internal deployment steps. How to tell whether you can use something For installation requirements and current limits, see Feature status.

en.title: Project DAG
en.description: Aggregate project goals, claims, review status, and decisions across sessions.
en.body: Project DAG Project DAG combines the evidence from several sessions in the same project, to help you see which conclusions the project has so far and which questions still need review. First update and save the evidence graph in each session's Evidence DAG, then come back to the project graph and click Update now . After a session saves new evidence, the project graph still has to be updated manually. Opening it - Entry: the Project DAG panel on the right; you can also open the matching view from a project, goal, or historical snapshot. - Target: the project that corresponds to the current workspace, and the evidence graphs each session has saved. - Prerequisite: the project has at least one saved session evidence graph, and the evidence-graph and project-graph features are available. Update and review the project graph 1. Finish the analysis in each session, save the sources and results, and update Evidence DAG for each. Wait until each session's evidence graph has finished saving. 2. Open the Project DAG, fill in the title and description under Project goal , and click Save goal . 3. Click Update now , wait for queueing, execution, and saving to all finish, then check this project graph. Only saving session evidence or closing the panel does not generate a new project graph automatically. 4. See how many items need attention, and the matching audit status and review package. Select an important conclusion and check which sources it rests on, whether it can be traced back to the original records, whether it can be rerun under the original conditions, and what evidence is still missing. 5. When you need to check details, open the matching session's Evidence DAG. After adding sources or results, first save the session evidence graph, then update the project graph manually. When reviewing - Confirm you are reviewing the graph from this update. After a new graph is saved, the old graph's audit results are marked stale, and you should recheck against the current graph. - The audit checks a project graph that is already saved. An audit failure does not undo a graph that was saved, and it does not modify conclusions directly. - Sources you are not allowed to view have their content hidden, and only limited status and gap hints are shown. When reviewing, note which parts could not be checked. - The project graph uses the evidence graphs each session has saved; analysis results that are not yet saved need to be organized in the session first. Saving and sharing Saving a goal and updating the project graph adds project records, so you can review them later. Operations in the panel act on the local project records; publishing or sending content out still needs authorization as the app requires. Before sharing, check source permissions, and state the unverified conclusions and the evidence gaps. Related pages - Evidence & Reproducibility: the group overview and the recommended record chain. - Evidence DAG: save the session evidence the project graph needs. - Research Dossier: turn research results into a readable deliverable. - Workspaces and sessions: how several sessions share one project scope. - Permissions & security: access permissions and publication authorization.

en.title: Research Checkpoints
en.description: Automatically save the summary, sources, and file references of completed research turns, to review and continue later.
en.body: Research Checkpoints Research Checkpoints automatically saves the chat turns that were accepted and completed, recording the research summary, the reasons for changes, the sources, and the related file and Git references. It helps you see what was done at the time, what it was based on, and where to continue next time. The record also hints at which operations were not fully recorded. Opening it - Entry: This turn's research record on a session result card; the card offers Open research dossier . - Target: the completed chat turns in the current session, and the workspace they are bound to. - Prerequisite: automatic recording is on by default and the session is bound to a workspace; the first version is generated after the first turn finishes. View and continue the research 1. Finish a round of research in a session bound to a workspace, and wait for the result card to show that the record has been saved. 2. Look at the title, the reason for changes, and the inputs and outputs, and check whether the sources and related files match this round's work. 3. Look for prompts that an analysis cannot be rerun, or that a result cannot be traced to its sources. When the operation record is incomplete, add the actual commands, environment, and output, so it can be rechecked later. 4. Under Exact artifact versions , choose an output and click Open to check the actual version it references. 5. Click Open research dossier to read the full record; to pick up from a historical record, select it and restore it as a new version, which keeps the existing history. What is saved A checkpoint saves the summary and the references. The actual file contents and artifact versions must be saved and checked separately, see Artifact Versions; for the Git state of the whole workspace, see Git Checkpoints. Having only a research summary does not mean all the result files were kept. Saving a record reads this round's conversation, the tool results, the workspace file changes, and the related artifact, computation, and Git records, and adds a checkpoint version. Existing versions are kept. When a record's ownership cannot yet be confirmed, it shows as pending, and you should check it before continuing. Manage automatic recording In the research dossier, use Turn on automatic recording or Stop automatic recording . Turns completed while recording is stopped are not recorded automatically afterwards. On a version conflict, you can save again based on the current version, or discard this round's record. Importing an old session, handling a conflict, and restoring as a new version need confirmation. Importing an old session keeps only the chat content; the system still warns that the history is incomplete and that some results cannot be traced to sources. The import itself does not fill in the research process that was missing at the time. Tips - Only chat turns that were accepted and completed are recorded; for a task not yet finished, wait until it completes before checking. - Operations done through the terminal, an editor, or similar may be recorded only as what changed, not fully as how those results were produced. Check them against the actual files and run records. - New checkpoints are visible only within the workspace and cannot be exported by default. Before sharing, check access permissions and the record contents. - The record redacts some narrative text, URLs, and credential-like query parameters, but you should still check manually for sensitive information. Related pages - Evidence & Reproducibility: the group overview and the recommended record chain. - Research Dossier: view records, control automatic recording, and restore historical versions. - Git Checkpoints: save a Git snapshot of the workspace. - Artifact Versions: save the content and versions of related artifacts. - Workspaces and sessions: how a session limits the scope of records.

en.title: Research Dossier
en.description: Turn the research question, inputs, methods, results, and limitations into a readable deliverable.
en.body: Research Dossier The research dossier puts the research summary, sources, key artifacts, versions, and limitations together, for review and delivery. After opening a research record, read the results and the limitations that need attention first, then look at earlier versions as needed. Process records come from Research Checkpoints, and evidence relationships are in Evidence DAG. Opening it - Entry: Research in the right toolbar (expand More tools if it is not shown); the right panel is titled Research as well; you can also click Open research dossier on a session result card. - To see history, open a specific artifact version or research record, and first confirm which record you are reading. - Prerequisite: the session is bound to a workspace; after research checkpoints or artifact versions have been saved, you can view the matching detailed records. The research dossier brings the research narrative, version position, credibility summary, and the limitations to consider onto one reading surface. Read and check a record 1. Finish a round of research, and click Open research dossier on the result card. 2. Confirm the selected research record and version, and read the overview, research sources, declared files, and key artifacts. 3. Look at Limitations to consider and Provenance breakpoints , and check item by item the missing sources, unverified results, and reproduction conditions. 4. To review history, load earlier versions in the Versions area, and use Compare exact version to check the differences. 5. When you need an earlier result, choose Restore as new version and confirm, then check the restored result and the actual files. The existing history is kept. When the selected record is missing or fails verification, the dossier shows a prompt. Check the record and the related files, and use it for delivery only after the problem is resolved. Preview and delivery Use Open verified preview to view the selected content, or Export Bundle V2 to package it for delivery. Exporting writes workspace files and asks for confirmation; check that all the required related versions and files are present and allowed to be accessed and exported, and state what has not yet been verified. Before sharing, also check the bundle for sensitive data. Restoring and importing an old session need confirmation as prompted. An imported old session stays marked as having an incomplete history, with the missing provenance information flagged. You can also turn automatic recording on or off here; for its behavior, see Research Checkpoints. Tips - What is shown depends on the checkpoints, artifact versions, and evidence the task has saved. If there are no records yet, finish and save a round of the task first. - When part of the record cannot be read for the moment, the matching content may be unavailable, while the rest of the verified content can still be read. - Empty blocks and inapplicable compute, evidence, or review blocks are omitted. Open Evidence DAG when you need the full evidence relationships. - The summaries and references in the dossier need to be checked against the actual files, especially after the related files were modified, moved, or deleted. Related pages - Evidence & Reproducibility: the group overview and the recommended record chain. - Research Checkpoints: save the research-process records in the dossier. - Artifact Versions: view, compare, and restore artifact versions. - Evidence DAG: see the complete in-session evidence relationships. - Feature status and limitations: see how far each feature is available.

en.title: Running analysis and computation
en.description: Run analysis in a Python, R, or cluster environment you configured, and keep the inputs, dependencies, and actual outputs.
en.body: Running analysis and computation Before running an analysis, prepare and verify the Python, R, or cluster environment you configured yourself. When you want the Agent to execute, state in the session the environment to use, the input files, the analysis steps, and the output location; which operations are available depends on the execution environment and permissions. 1. Confirm the location, format, and version of the input files, and keep the raw data and source records. 2. Prepare the scripts and the dependencies they need, and record the interpreter, package versions, and run parameters; for cluster jobs, also record the submit command and resource requests. 3. Actually run the analysis, and check the run status, exit code, and logs; on failure, keep the error message, fix it, and run again. 4. Check that the output files and statistical results match expectations, and save how the inputs, code, dependencies, and outputs correspond. Without an actual run record, do not write an expected result up as a completed computation. To plot from data and Python code, revise, and accept candidate figures, use Scientific Figures; that plugin must be installed separately with its dependencies configured, and currently supports Python + Matplotlib. For cross-task source and computation records, see Evidence & reproducibility.

en.title: Scientific Figures
en.description: Select files, describe the plot you want in chat, really run Python, and compare and accept candidate figures.
en.body: Scientific Figures Select files → tell the AI how to draw → review the result → accept when satisfied. Scientific Figures ties a text request, Python code, an actual run, and image versions together. To revise a figure, describe the change you want in the input box. Prepare Python and Matplotlib before use. Python plotting is currently supported; R and MATLAB are not. Plotting execution in SciForge currently runs only on macOS environments that pass the safety check; on Windows and Linux, installing the plugin still does not let you run plotting through this entry. For cases and screenshots of multi-file cleaning, four-panel figures, missing-value matrices, and failure recovery, see the Scientific figures case. Installing and opening 1. In Extensions → Marketplace , find the Scientific Figures package compatible with your SciForge version, check the publisher and permissions, approve the installation, and enable it. If it is not listed, the maintainer must supply a signed package and its installation source. 2. Open a writable local workspace and a DSH session whose model is configured. 3. In SciForge, select Scientific Figures from the plugin picker in the right sidebar. In native DSH, use the Figures panel in the session input area, or type /scientific-figures . The default Figure page contains file input, text input, and image preview. First confirm that the chosen Python has Matplotlib installed, then run a simple plotting task to check the environment. You can point to the interpreter with pythonCommand in the plugin configuration. <details <summary Version and package compatibility requirements</summary Native DSH requires =0.2.1-rc.4 <0.3.0 and Node =22. The package contains the native Canvas component for this platform, so a different platform, architecture, or Linux libc needs a matching build; installing successfully does not mean the current system can run plotting. </details Starting from data and code Data and code are the core of reproducibility; the image is the result of one run. First put the files in the current workspace, then under New choose the files and a starting point: Starting point Must provide What happens next --- --- --- Start from data (recommended) Data file, plotting request The AI inspects the data, writes code, saves a copy of this step's data, actually runs it, and creates the first figure. Existing data and code Data file, Python code, request Saves the code and a copy of the data, runs once to get a result you can compare against later; an existing image can also be provided for comparison. After you click Start plotting , check the run results in the session on the left; when it finishes, refresh and select the figure. Later, keep typing changes on the Figure page; you do not need to reselect every raw data file. text Read data/trend.csv, use time as the x-axis and response as the y-axis. Draw a blue line chart with units on the axes. Do not fabricate data. Save this step's data and code and actually run it; for later changes, generate a candidate first and wait for my confirmation. With only an image, the exact data cannot be recovered. An original image you provide is marked "user-supplied, not yet verified" and linked to the saved code and inputs; the image generated by an actual run is saved separately, which makes it easy to tell them apart and compare. Saving and reusing data Every change saves the code and a copy of the data, and records which file was run, which parameters were used, and which version this change was based on. Old code, run results, and images can still be viewed in the history. If the original file is later rewritten or deleted, the data of a saved version does not change. Later changes keep using the last saved copy of the data by default. To use the latest data in the workspace instead, tick Re-read workspace data in advanced settings, then save a new version. If cleaned, filtered, or transformed data should feed the next step, first save it as a file, then choose that file as the input; variables in Python memory do not automatically become the next step's data. Rerunning a specific version uses the code, parameters, and data copy saved with that version. Analysis files, history, and recovery Besides images, you can also save analysis files such as a cleaned CSV, statistics JSON, and text notes. When you need to continue the analysis, have the AI find which files a given run saved, then choose the files you need as the next step's input. Only PNGs can be published as figures; other files let you see their saved path and summary. <details <summary Referencing analysis files by hand, and format limits</summary When writing a script, write analysis files such as cleaned.csv , summary.json , and rules.txt to SCIENTIFIC_FIGURES_OUTPUT_DIR . To reference one by hand, first have the AI list the files and confirm which run's file to use, then take the workspace-relative path .scientific-figures/ plus the output.path returned for that file, and put it into inputPaths of the new code version, which saves an input copy for the next step. CSV/TSV/TXT must be valid UTF-8, and JSON must be parseable; a file that does not meet this fails to save. PNGs: at most 16, 20 MiB each, 64 MiB in total; analysis files: at most 32, 8 MiB each, 32 MiB in total. </details Code and runs shows 20 summary entries per page; click More code versions / More runs to see the next page; after selecting a record you can see its details. If one record is damaged, an error is shown and the other records can still be viewed. If a run has already ended but its results are not yet saved, you can look at the record under Code and runs → Runs that have not finished or were interrupted . Complete interrupted record is offered only when the recorded results can confirm the run ended; it saves the existing results without rerunning Python. When there is no result you can confirm, when it cannot be confirmed that Python has stopped, or when the record is reported still occupied, this step cannot be completed; when a run fails, you still need to fix the problem and run it again. Rebuilding the environment After a successful run, the Python and dependency versions, system information, and environment rebuild notes are saved. To rebuild the environment, create a separate environment and install the dependencies as described in _environment/REBUILD.md in the run directory; requirements.txt in the same directory records the exact package versions, and environment.json records the environment information. After changing the system or the Python version, recheck the results; system libraries and drivers you must prepare yourself. Revising, comparing, and accepting Keep describing changes in words, for example "keep the data, make the line blue, and shorten the title". The AI saves a new code version, actually runs it, and publishes the output as a candidate figure. - Current figure / After change : compare the current figure with the selected candidate. When there are several candidates, switch among them in the Candidates drop-down. - Request acceptance : sends the acceptance request to the session; check the candidate figure in the session, then click Allow to make it the current figure. - Keep current figure : decline the selected candidate and keep using the current figure. After accepting, the earlier images, code, and run records are still kept. If the current figure changes again after a candidate is generated, regenerate the candidate based on the figure as it is now. Viewing code and runs Open Code and runs when you need to check the process; ordinary plotting does not need you to read this first. 1. Select a version and click Load version to see the Python source. 2. After editing, click Save and freeze code to save a new version. 3. Click Run frozen Python to see the run status and output. Parameters, input files, code comparison, environment, and logs can be expanded as needed. 4. A successful output can be published as a new figure. To publish it as a candidate of an existing figure, first check and confirm which current figure you are changing, then publish the candidate. You can also expand All versions and sources to see the code and run records linked to a specific figure. Case: revise a line chart and keep the history For a line chart with x-axis [1, 2, 3] and y-axis [1, 3, 8] , you can ask to keep the x-axis and change the y-axis to [2, 4, 7] . The plugin saves the changed code and actually runs it, producing a candidate image you can compare with the current figure. After checking the result, go through Request acceptance → Allow to make the candidate the current figure. The original figure and the code from before the change are kept; after reopening the workspace, you can still view the accepted figure and the history. Common problems What you see What to do --- --- The AI finished but the panel still shows the old figure Click Refresh , and check the figure and the candidate selection. Sending fails Confirm there is an available DSH session and model connection; keep your input and retry after the session recovers. Python or Matplotlib is unavailable Look at the error under Code and runs , configure the correct interpreter and dependencies, then retry with a new run. The image auto-attachment shows File not found Ask the AI to read that run again; if it still cannot be shown, check that the image file exists and confirm the plugin version. You cannot accept a candidate Check whether you clicked Allow in the session, and whether the current figure has changed; regenerate the candidate if needed. A run failed but you still want to publish an image Fix it and run successfully first; a failed run cannot be published as a formal candidate. Current scope and limits - You can describe plotting and revision requests in words, save images, analysis files, code, and data copies, view history, recover results from a run that has ended but not been saved, and compare and accept candidate figures. - Input files must be in the current workspace. After a successful plot you must refresh manually; local dependencies and the model service are yours to configure. - Records are saved in .scientific-figures/ in the current workspace; when you want to use them in other artifact or evidence panels, organize the linked records separately. - The first session limits the writable scope of the workspace; switching directories does not widen permissions. Running is refused in a read-only environment, when isolation is unavailable, or when the workspace is in the system temporary directory. - Local Python has write isolation, but it may still read other files or access the network. Model requests are also subject to the data policy of the model service you use. Only run trusted code. Related pages - Extension Center: installation sources, permissions, and enabling/disabling. - Runtime and models: prepare a working session. - Workspaces and sessions: confirm files and task context. - Feature status and limitations: verified scope and release status. - Version & Compatibility: version information and compatibility requirements.

en.title: SiYuan Notes
en.description: Connect your own SiYuan service to the workbench and archive traceable Markdown summaries after tasks finish.
en.body: SiYuan Notes SiYuan Notes connects a user-provided remote SiYuan service to the workbench as a full-page editor for reading, editing, and archiving research records. It is used in the organization stage after task execution, and you can also consult notes during a task. SciForge does not bundle the kernel or run or manage that service for you. How to open it - Entry: SiYuan Notes in the left sidebar opens the editor to the right of the session by default. From the page header you can move it to the left, bottom, or main area and resize it. Position and size are saved on this machine. - Target: the SiYuan service you run or subscribe to, along with its notebooks and documents. - Prerequisite: an accessible HTTP/HTTPS SiYuan address. If the service requires authentication, enter an API token in the page's settings, or use the SIYUAN_API_TOKEN environment variable. SciForge does not start or distribute the SiYuan kernel with the app. What you can do What you want to do How to do it Output --- --- --- Connect your own SiYuan Enter the service address in Settings on the page and save it; leave it blank to use the installation default An editor session that persists across restarts Edit and browse notes Use the SiYuan interface directly in the full-page editor Document changes in SiYuan Search and read existing notes Ask the Agent to search by path fragment, then read by document ID or path The note location and Markdown body; long notes are marked as truncated Archive task summaries automatically For a top-level Agent turn that finishes successfully and produces a final reply, SciForge writes an entry to a notebook automatically A Markdown document in SciForge 工作总结 , containing the request, final reply, time, and turn identifier Have the Agent write to a specific document Ask the Agent to save results to SiYuan and provide the title, notebook, and path The target document in SiYuan Typical workflow 1. First confirm in the SiYuan service that the target notebook exists and is writable. If authentication is required, prepare an API token and save it in the page's settings or set it in the launch environment. 2. Open SiYuan Notes from the left sidebar and enter the service address in Settings. If the page reports an error, retry or open Settings to correct it. 3. Read or edit in the editor. Do not place sensitive content that should not leave the local machine into a remote service. 4. After an Agent task completes normally, check whether a corresponding record appears under SciForge 工作总结 . If the service is temporarily unreachable, records queue and retry. Where things are saved, and what actions affect - Content you read and edit comes from the connected SiYuan service. The API token saved in the page's settings is used first; otherwise the environment variable is used. A token entered on the page is kept in the app's encrypted storage. - Automatic archiving saves to a fixed notebook in SiYuan; when you ask the Agent to write a document, state the title, notebook, and path. - Archiving after a successful task is sent to the configured SiYuan service automatically, without asking each time. Before use, confirm the service address, the range of notes it can access, and which content is suitable to send to that service. - When the service is unreachable, pending archives stay on this machine waiting to be retried; the official notes still need to be written to the SiYuan service successfully. Known limitations - Server mode only: you must provide an accessible SiYuan service, and the address must be HTTP/HTTPS. - Content Space currently lists only the notebooks that are open in SiYuan; to read, edit, and search documents, use the SiYuan page or the Agent's tools. Content Space cannot upload or download files. - Automatic archiving covers only successful top-level Agent turns. Intermediate progress, failures, cancellations, and continuous sub-turns are not archived, and it does not produce a second AI summary or claim that the task is verified. - Archiving writes to the fixed notebook SciForge 工作总结 and the /SciForge path; the notebook is created if it does not exist. Before retrying the same task turn, it checks whether the matching task note already exists, to avoid creating duplicates. - SciForge does not ship the SiYuan kernel; using it on this machine also means deploying the service yourself. - When the service is unreachable or a write result is uncertain, pending records are kept locally and retried on the next task or at startup. Unconfirmed writes are not repeated blindly. Related pages - Content Space: choose a SiYuan notebook from the connected service. - Collaboration: collaborative delivery and post-task local archiving are two different paths. - Permissions and security: external service addresses, tokens, and data boundaries. - Feature status and limitations: the capability scope of the first version. Implementation basis: @sciforge/domain-siyuan-content-space-provider v0.3.1.

en.title: Terminal
en.description: Run commands directly in the workspace, verify the results, and keep key output in the session.
en.body: Terminal Terminal puts the command-line environment for the current workspace in the bottom panel. It is suited to running scripts, checking logs, and confirming the status of long-running tasks. You type commands in the panel yourself; when the Agent runs commands in a session, it follows the Runtime's approval and sandbox policies. The permission settings for the two apply separately. How to open it - Entry: Terminal in the right toolbar (expand More tools if it is not shown), or Terminal in the bottom panel. - Target: the current workspace. The terminal process uses the workspace root as its initial working directory. - Prerequisite: a workspace is open, and the local or remote Workspace Host can start a system shell. - Tabs: a workspace can have multiple tabs (up to 8), with support for renaming, closing other tabs, closing all tabs, and restarting the process. What you can do What you want to do How to do it Output --- --- --- Run a one-off command Enter a command in a tab and press Enter Terminal output and the process exit status Watch a long-running task Keep the tab open and scroll through the ongoing output Task progress; closing the tab ends that terminal process Separate tasks Create and name separate tabs Command-line sessions isolated by tab Reproduce experiment steps Put the commands in a script, run it in the terminal, and record key output Commands you can run again, plus exit statuses Typical workflow 1. Confirm that the workspace shown at the top is the project this task should work on. 2. Open Terminal and run pwd and read-only commands first to confirm the directory, interpreter, and dependencies. 3. For commands that will write files, access the network, or install software, check the target paths, arguments, and recovery plan first. 4. Explain the purpose of the command in the session, and bring key output, exit statuses, or error messages back into the conversation. 5. Check the file state after the task. Copy terminal content you need to keep into notes or an artifact. Inputs, outputs, and permissions - Reads: commands can read files, environment variables, and network resources that the current user has permission to access. - Writes: commands can modify workspace files and may also write outside the workspace. The working directory is not a filesystem sandbox. - Approval or external effects: Terminal does not prompt for each command. Operations such as installing dependencies, accessing the network, and overwriting files take effect directly under the current user's permissions. - Agent execution: commands started by the Agent are governed by its Runtime's approval and sandbox settings. There is no promise that all commands skip approval, and no guarantee that every command triggers a prompt. - Output retention: commands and output stay with the tab in the current workspace and are not kept after the tab closes. Results from Agent-started commands return to the session context with the tool call. - What it does not do: it does not automatically write terminal content into the conversation record. Closing a tab ends the corresponding terminal process, but switching workspaces does not automatically end terminals that are already running. Known limitations - Terminal processes in remote workspaces run remotely, and output is read through incremental cursors. Remote controlled terminals are pipe-based and do not claim full pseudo-terminal (PTY) compatibility. - The tab limit is 8. Closing all tabs collapses the panel, and unsaved screen content is not restored. - Command availability depends on the shell, PATH, and dependencies on the local or remote host. SciForge does not install missing tools for you. - Terminal scrollback is limited. Write important output to files or logs, and use persistent scheduling or logging for long-running tasks. - Content in the manual terminal does not automatically enter the Agent context. To inform the Agent, paste the necessary excerpts into the session or have it run the commands itself. Related pages - Workbench tools: how files, Terminal, Browser, and Computer Use divide responsibilities. - Workspaces and sessions: workspace locations and session state. - Permissions and security: approvals, credentials, and the scope of command effects. - Remote resources and collaboration: terminals and data boundaries in remote workspaces. Implementation basis: @sciforge/domain-terminal v1.0.1.

en.title: View and revise figures
en.description: Describe figure changes in words, then compare and accept the candidate after it actually runs.
en.body: View and revise figures Use the standalone Scientific Figures plugin to generate figures from data and Python + Matplotlib code. Install a compatible plugin and prepare the environment it needs first, then state the plotting or revision request in words. 1. Choose the data and code in the workspace, and say what to change, for example "keep the data, make the line blue, and shorten the title". With only an image, the exact data cannot be recovered. 2. Have the Agent save a new code version and actually run it, check the run status and the output, and generate a candidate figure once it succeeds. 3. Compare the current version and the candidate under Current figure / After change ; when there are several candidates, switch among them in the Candidates drop-down. 4. When satisfied, click Request acceptance , then go to the session, check the figure, and click Allow to make the candidate the current figure; to keep revising, state the next request. The plugin keeps immutable code, input, run, and image versions; accepting a candidate updates the current figure, while the original figure and the run records are kept. After a figure changes, a candidate may need to be regenerated. It has no on-image boxes, arrows, or pins for annotation, and it does not register records with artifact versions or evidence relationships automatically. To leave feedback on specific text, use the standalone Anchored Comments. When you need a screenshot, enable that feature first. A comment only records feedback; changing the image still requires running the plot again and accepting the candidate. For organizing and delivering results, see Evidence & reproducibility.

en.title: Five-minute quickstart
en.description: Open a local project, analyze it read-only with Codex, and verify the file state before and after the task.
en.body: Five-minute quickstart Start by having the Agent examine a local project in read-only mode: open a workspace, confirm Codex's permissions, send a task, then compare the file state. When you are done, you should see a project overview and no changes to project files. 1. Prepare a project and a model Start SciForge, prepare a clean Git project or a copy of a project, and configure working model access and Codex. For the first run you can start from a local workspace without signing in to the collaboration cloud. In the first-run wizard or Settings → General , choose Model API or Coding Plan . Then go to Settings → AI assistant and check whether Codex is detected. Settings is at the bottom of the expanded left sidebar; account and cloud status are in the same area. Illustrates the two paths, Model API and Coding Plan. 2. Record the file state and set read-only permissions Run this in the project directory and save the output: bash git status --short If there are already modifications, record them clearly first; for a non-Git project, use a copy. Go to Settings → AI assistant → Codex and set File access range to Can only read files , keeping an appropriate tool approval policy. Wait for the setting to apply, finish any existing tasks, then reconnect or restart and start a new session. “Can edit workspace” in the figure allows writes; change it to “Can only read files” before starting this tutorial. For detailed steps, see configure a read-only sandbox. Write the no-modification instruction into the prompt as well; if you see a request to widen permissions, stop and check, because this task needs no write access. 3. Open a local workspace and start a new session In the Workspace location menu, choose Local workspace, open the project directory, and check the path and the project name on the left. Start a new session, and confirm in the bottom input area that the execution runtime is Codex . The left side of the current workbench is for project, session, and collaboration navigation; the vertical toolbar on the far right opens tools such as files, and panels dock beside it. If there are many tools, open More tools . Shows a local project and a new session. 4. Send your first task Enter: Look at the current workspace, list only the top-level files and directories, and describe in one sentence what this project might be. Do not modify files or install dependencies. You do not need to add attachments for this task. To point at an existing file, use the file panel's reference action or type @ . Choosing files from outside your machine, dragging them in, or pasting images may import files into the workspace first, which changes the file baseline for the read-only check; save that for a later task. For the difference between the attachment tray and the labels on sent files, see workspaces and sessions. Shows the task text and the execution runtime. After sending, watch the tool calls, working directory, and execution results in the session. If the Runtime is not connected, check Settings → AI assistant and the model configuration first, then send again. Shows the execution state within the same session. 5. Verify the results and files The answer should list the top-level contents and give a grounded judgment about what the project is. Run again: bash git status --short Compare with the pre-task state and confirm that no project files were added, deleted, or modified. Git does not show ignored caches; when you need a strict check, also compare your copy's file list and content hashes. If you find changes, stop and investigate rather than restoring existing modifications outright. Viewing the analysis result in the session. Once you confirm that the workspace is correct, Codex responds normally, read-only permissions are applied, and the file state matches the pre-task state, you have completed your first task. Next, you can continue with: Continue the read-only analysis. Explain what the main directories are for, the likely entry files, and a recommended way to start or test the project. List anything that cannot be confirmed from the source separately. Do not modify files or install dependencies. Continue reading: Runtime and model access, working with the Agent.

en.title: Configure a read-only sandbox
en.description: Configure Codex's read-only execution scope, understand how Claude Plan mode differs, and compare Git status before and after a task.
en.body: Configure a read-only sandbox “Do not modify files” in a prompt is a task requirement; you also need to configure execution permissions. This page uses the Codex read-only sandbox as the getting-started path; the file-scope option of the same name in Claude Code corresponds to Plan mode , and the two isolate work differently. Where the setting lives 1. Expand the left sidebar and open Settings from the bottom. 2. Go to AI assistant . 3. In the AI assistant configuration cards at the top of the page, find Codex . 4. Find the File access range dropdown under that Runtime and select Can only read files . 5. Wait for the setting to apply, then reconnect or restart SciForge after finishing the current task; do not keep using a running task whose permissions are not yet confirmed. 6. Return to the workbench, start a new session, and confirm in the bottom-right of the input box that the execution runtime is codex . The Access shortcut at the top of the page jumps to the Computer Use configuration; the file access range is in each Runtime's own configuration section. The value shown allows workspace changes; select “Can only read files” for read-only tasks. Runtime What “Can only read files” actually means Boundaries --- --- --- Codex Requests Codex's readOnly sandbox and disables command network access within that sandbox Suitable for the local file inspection in this tutorial; stop and check any request that widens permissions Claude Code Uses Claude Code's plan permission mode For analysis and planning; do not claim it provides the same filesystem sandbox isolation as Codex DSH Has no file access range option of the same name; the native shell is off by default and, once enabled for a DSH you installed, approved command by command This tutorial uses Codex; do not treat DSH's shell switch as a filesystem read-only sandbox MCP, remote commands, and Computer Use permissions must each be checked separately; for your first task, use only the tools needed to read the local project. Adding files from outside the workspace, dragging files in, or pasting images may import files into the workspace first. For a read-only check, reference existing files and record the baseline again once the import completes. Removing an attachment above the input box only cancels this send; it does not delete files that have already been imported. What read-only mode allows You can usually: - List directories and read text files - Search source and configuration - View Git status and diffs - Run checks that do not write to the workspace - Provide analyses, plans, and recommendations You should not allow: - Creating, overwriting, renaming, or deleting files - Installing dependencies that write to the project - Running commands that generate caches, logs, or build artifacts - Modifying the Git index, commits, or branches Whether a command is truly read-only depends on what it does, not what it is called. Some tests and interpreters generate caches automatically; if you hit a write failure in the read-only sandbox, change your checking approach rather than widening permissions just to finish the tutorial. Double verification In a Git project, run this before and after the task: bash git status --short Comparing Git status detects changes but does not replace execution isolation; it also does not list files ignored by .gitignore . When you need a strict check of every file, use a copy of the project and additionally compare the file list and content hashes before and after the task. If the output changes: 1. Stop any further tasks immediately. 2. Have the Agent list the changes, and check the file differences with git diff . 3. Do not automatically delete or restore existing modifications. 4. Determine whether the changes come from the task, from tool caches, or already existed before the task. When to switch to workspace write Switch to Can edit workspace only when a task explicitly needs to generate scripts, tables, figures, or documents and you have checked the plan and output paths. Write tasks should use a project copy or a clean branch, and you should review the changes when finished. Next: working with the Agent.

en.title: Runtime and model access
en.description: Configure model access, choose Codex, Claude Code, or DeepSeek Harness, and complete a connection check.
en.body: Runtime and model access Configure the model service first, then choose the AI assistant that executes tasks. The former determines where model requests go; the latter plans work and calls tools. Setting Entry point What to confirm --- --- --- Model access First-run wizard or Settings → General The Model API base URL, key, and model, or official sign-in for Coding Plan AI assistant Settings → AI assistant Installation, connection, and permissions for Codex, Claude Code, or DeepSeek Harness (DSH) Current session Execution settings in the bottom input area The Runtime, model, and available tiers for this run Settings is at the bottom of the expanded left sidebar. Local accounts and SciForge cloud sign-in are managed separately, see Identity & Access. Choose model access With Model API , enter the Base URL, API Key, and model name provided by your service provider; if you are unsure about the protocol, use automatic detection. An existing key only means the field is configured; whether the upstream accepts it must be confirmed with an actual request. Use it only to recognize the fields; enter your own service configuration. With Coding Plan , complete official sign-in or device-code authorization in the interface. The Coding Plan path currently supports Codex; Claude Code uses model access. If sign-in or connection fails, fix the current access path according to the prompt, then retry. Choose and connect a Runtime In Settings → AI assistant , choose the execution runtime and check the detection result; if automatic detection fails, use Choose local app or enter the absolute path to the executable, then detect again. - Codex : uses the installed Codex app-server; check the model and permissions before starting a task. - Claude Code : configure model access and check its permission mode. - DSH : connects through a local ACP program; the model and reasoning tier take effect in the session after connecting. Check the program you specified, the system path, and common install locations first, and only try the component bundled with the app when none of them work. DSH's Shell command execution is off by default; enable it only for a DSH you installed yourself, and each run still requires approval. Do not switch to full permissions just to make an error go away. Shows execution runtime configuration, tool confirmations, and file scope. Codex and Claude Code can edit the workspace by default. For your first analysis, adjust permissions according to configure a read-only sandbox first. After switching execution runtimes, re-check the connection, sign-in, and permissions; existing sessions' mappings and configuration do not migrate automatically. When you need to operate desktop applications, also check Computer Use 's Runtime support, backend, and system permissions. Illustrates the configuration items that must be checked separately. Run a minimal connection check Start a new session, confirm that the expected Runtime is selected in the input area, and send: Reply only with “connected”. Do not read or modify files, and do not call external services. After you receive a response, continue to the five-minute quickstart. If the selected Runtime is unavailable, fix it according to the error or switch deliberately; the app will not automatically pick another Runtime for you. Troubleshoot DSH timeouts DSH distinguishes between a timeout on a single connection request and a task that makes no progress for a long time: Case Meaning and handling --- --- Initialization, create, or resume session requests time out The default single wait is 15 seconds. Check the local program, the connection, and any explicit error; extending the wait will not solve long-running tasks A task produces no session updates for a long time By default, the turn stops after 10 minutes of continuous silence; long tasks that keep receiving updates for the current session can exceed 10 minutes. Review the existing results before deciding whether to continue the same session For technical troubleshooting: the former's configuration name is requestTimeoutMs ; the latter, although named promptTimeoutMs , means the idle limit and has the error code runtime_prompt_idle_timeout . After a timeout, the original session identifier can be recovered, but you should still check existing files and external actions before continuing the task.

en.title: SciForge User Manual
en.description: From opening a project and handing the AI a task to checking results, saving records, and collaborating with your team.
en.body: SciForge User Manual In SciForge, you can open a project, let the AI read materials, modify files, run analyses, and create figures, then check the results and request changes. The files, conversations, and run records from a task remain available for review and for later collaboration. If this is your first time, start with the five-minute quickstart. If you already have a specific question, use the outline below to find the right page; there is no need to read the whole manual from beginning to end. The manual has six parts Part When to read it What it covers --- --- --- Getting started The first time you open SciForge Connect a model, choose an execution runtime, open a project, and complete a simple task; set read-only access or allow file changes. Workbench guides You want to know where a button is or how to hand files to the AI Workspaces and sessions, adding attachments, file preview, panel layout, Terminal and Browser Preview, as well as how to describe a task and check results. Features & Extensions You need to complete a particular kind of research work Scientific file preview, plotting and comments, versions and research records, team collaboration, notes, scheduled tasks, and extensions. Case tutorials You want to see how a complete task is done From input data through running an analysis, revising results, and delivering them; includes scientific plotting, multi-person RNA-seq collaboration, and virtual cell cases. Settings & security You need to adjust file access, tool permissions, or connected services File and network access, action confirmations, and the conditions for using remote resources and team collaboration. Reference & troubleshooting You hit an error or a version mismatch, or need to look up installation requirements Troubleshooting, versions and compatibility, feature limits, and extension licenses. Find a page by goal - Have the AI read a project first : five-minute quickstart. - Hand files to the AI and continue an earlier conversation : workspaces and sessions. - Open a sequence, molecular structure, or omics file : Life Science Preview. - Plot from data, then refine step by step : Scientific Figures. - See which files changed and save intermediate results : Evidence & Reproducibility. - Invite members, assign tasks, and review deliverables : team collaboration. - Install extensions or connect external tools : extensions and marketplace. - The interface does not match the tutorial : versions and compatibility. A few names to start with Name Meaning --- --- Workspace The project directory you open, which holds the files a task uses. Session A conversation around one task, which you can come back to and continue at any time. Runtime (execution runtime) The program that handles tasks; you can choose Codex, Claude Code, or DSH. For configuration, see Runtime and model access. Research records Keep intermediate results, the run process, and the basis for conclusions, so you can look them up and continue later.

en.title: Documentation maintenance checklist
en.description: Maintain one user manual against the latest client, and check versions, links, and the public boundary.
en.body: Documentation maintenance checklist User tutorials are maintained only in sciforge-docs-v2 . The client repository keeps the site entry points, install and development notes, and internal supplements; it no longer duplicates the full tutorials. 1. Pin this round's version Record the date and commit of the latest client mainline first, then verify the interfaces, settings, package versions, and operations the change touches. Update Version and compatibility and the repository README. Record the public source commit separately; do not wait for it to update before writing the manual. Read the current implementation, not just the old README, test names, or planning documents. If a behavior exists only as a test expectation and is not wired into any actual call, list it as an item to verify; do not write it up as an operating step. 2. Update content and navigation - Write "where to open it, how to operate it, what you get" first, then the limits that affect the operation. - Use the actual names shown in the interface. Do not repeat the mainline commit, permission terms, and verification notes on every page; link to the version page instead. - When a feature moves, adjust the overview, sidebar, and related links. Keep a short migration note at the old URL and take it out of the current feature navigation. - English site: update the same-path pages under i18n/en/docusaurus-plugin-content-docs/current/ . When you add or remove a page or rename a sidebar category, also update i18n/en/docusaurus-plugin-content-docs/current.json . - Do not claim "all plugins are available" from a directory count. Describe built-in modules, standalone plugins, Skills, and MCP separately. - Keep the original date and version on screenshots and cases. Do not relabel them as a new-version demo unless re-recorded; add one sentence to outdated screens. 3. Check the public boundary The public site may describe user operations of the latest client. Internal deployment, database migration, VPN/SSH management, server-side adaptation, real account configuration, and private acceptance material stay in internal documents. General usage such as client sign-in, device connection, and team projects can be public. For new images, first check for visible accounts, paths, tokens, and rights to the material. Keep already-reviewed images; do not bulk-restore old media from the private repository. Keep plugin licenses, original-author attribution, and third-party notices as they are; documentation updates do not change licenses or repository visibility. 4. Keep entry points consistent The user-manual links on the public and private client home pages both point to https://agi4sci.github.io/sciforge-docs-v2/ . Old manual pages inside the repository keep a link to the matching site page. Internal supplements do not go into the public export. Later source exports must keep the licenses, replacement assets, security test fixtures, and these entry points that the public repository has already reviewed; do not overwrite the public repository with the private repository's directories. 5. Build and check bash npm ci npm run typecheck npm run build The build generates the search index and checks internal links. Also check whether retired features still appear on the home page, sidebar, search suggestions, and video chapter descriptions. A successful build only shows the docs can be built; the content still needs a page-by-page review. If the video is not re-recorded, keep the original file and chapter order, and note the applicable version on the guide page. When chapter data is involved, also run node scripts/check-tour.cjs . 6. Publish and spot-check Review through a PR, and wait for the GitHub Pages deployment to succeed after merging. Spot-check the home page, the version page, the feature overview, and this round's key pages online, and confirm the new content and page links work. The PR should state the basis for the update, the main pages, the check results, and any screenshots that need to be retaken later. If something goes wrong, roll back with a new revert PR; do not deploy an earlier site configuration.

en.title: Remote resources and collaboration
en.description: Distinguish remote workspace sessions from SciForge Cloud collaboration, and understand the data and permission boundaries of each.
en.body: Remote resources and collaboration Remote workspaces address "where compute and data live"; Cloud collaboration addresses "who works together around a Project and Task." The two can be combined or used independently. Remote workspaces A remote workspace brings a SciForge Workspace Host session running on another machine into the local workbench: files, terminals, Git, and Agent requests act on the remote directory, while the interface stays on your machine. - Entry point: the Workspace location selector at the top of the workbench, which switches between Local workspace and attached remote sessions; the selector also shows each remote session's lifecycle (Persistent server / Connection session), connection status (Remote, Reconnecting, Offline, Limited, Connection error), and network exit. - When a session disconnects or errors, use Reconnect on the target session in the selector. - The open-source client does not include a connection management panel for registering SSH targets, VPN environments, and workspace authorization; remote sessions appear in the selector only after the deployer provides and attaches them. Remote files, terminals, and Agent commands actually act on the remote directory. Do not mistake "displayed in a local window" for "the data has been copied to your machine." After connecting, check the remote path and file reads first, then test the terminal and the tools you need. If one tool reports that it is unavailable, do not conclude that the entire remote workspace is unusable; for the specific scope, see Version and compatibility. Cloud collaboration Use Cloud collaboration when you need to continue a personal Session on your phone, or when a team needs to assign and accept Tasks around a Project. It requires the Cloud service address, account, and collaboration service configuration provided by your administrator. For team procedures, see Collaboration guide; for a real submission, revision, and downstream handoff, see Pasilla three-person collaboration case. Check the sign-in and device prerequisites for team collaboration in that guide; setting up a personal Session on your phone is a separate path. Figure 2: Cloud connection status and the local workspace are independent of each other. Unified sign-in has three distinct states: State Purpose --- --- Local account Marks the current user and ownership on this machine Cloud sign-in Confirms your cloud identity Device connection Click Connect this device to authorize the current desktop installation to access Cloud capabilities A local account is not cloud authentication; a connected workspace also does not mean you have joined a collaboration Project. In collaboration, Shared files is for viewing resources provided by the content service; there is currently no direct upload entry point. Task delivery follows the Task submission and acceptance process; do not treat the Shared files entry as a general-purpose cloud drive upload. Figure 3: Team collaboration revolves around Projects, Tasks, owners, and acceptance results. Data and credential boundaries - SSH keys, VPN credentials, and MFA are managed by the user or by system security infrastructure. - Cloud, collaboration services, and Content Space may send data to external services. - Before uploading production data, confirm the destination, scope, retention policy, and team permissions. - Remote commands and collaborative tasks should still record inputs, outputs, return codes, and approvals. - After a network interruption, confirm the state of the remote process before deciding whether to retry, to avoid submitting compute twice. Case: Virtual cell perturbation prediction benchmark.

en.title: Permissions and security
en.description: Choose read-only, workspace write, approval, and Computer Use permissions according to the impact of the task.
en.body: Permissions and security First choose the file access range for the task, then check the terminal, plugin, remote service, and computer-use permissions you will use. Confirm the workspace and output locations before running, and verify the destination before submitting or uploading. File access range Range Suitable tasks Main risks --- --- --- Can only read files Project understanding, code review, data inventory, and planning Codex uses a read-only sandbox; Claude uses Plan mode, and the two are not equivalent Can edit workspace Modifying code and generating analyses, figures, and reports Overwriting existing files, writing to the wrong directory, and mixing in unrelated changes Can access all files Controlled tasks that explicitly require cross-directory reads or writes Removes read-only or workspace scope limits and runs tools automatically, potentially affecting data and configuration outside the workspace For a first task, an unfamiliar repository, or an unreviewed Skill, start with the Codex read-only configuration. Both Codex and Claude allow workspace writes in their initial configuration, so you must change this deliberately; MCP, remote execution, and Computer Use each require separate permission checks. For details, see Configuring a read-only sandbox. Approval policy An approval request should state at least: - What operation will be performed - The target files, directories, hosts, or external services - Whether it will write, upload, send, or delete - Whether it can be retried safely after a failure - How to check the result and recover The absence of an approval dialog does not mean an operation is read-only. Manual terminals run with the current system user's permissions; plugins must also be installed, enabled, and granted permissions for the relevant version separately. Credentials - Do not put API keys, tokens, or passwords in prompts, Git repositories, or screenshots. - MCP, the Model API, and collaboration services should each use the minimum credential scope they need. - Do not treat a provider key as a Runtime login credential. - Before exporting logs, traces, or a research dossier, check for Authorization headers, server addresses, real paths, and sample privacy. Computer Use Computer Use can operate supported web pages and in-app embedded pages. Before using it, check the run status in SciForge settings; macOS users also need to check the Screen Recording and Accessibility permissions. Figure 1: Before enabling it, check the chosen executor, the run status, and the system permissions. The following actions should be confirmed by the user at the moment they are performed: account sign-in or authorization, sending messages, uploading data, purchasing or paying, deleting external content, and submitting formal evaluation results. When Scientific Figures accepts a candidate figure, it requires a formal tool call in the session and host confirmation; "Request acceptance" in the panel only initiates the request. Deleting anchored comments and submitting feedback also have their own confirmation steps; see the corresponding feature pages for details. Research data security - Use public or redistributable data for tutorials. - Do not overwrite raw data by default; write derived results to a separate directory. - Whether data in a remote workspace may be downloaded is determined by the project policy. - External models, MCP, and web uploads change the data boundary and must be evaluated separately. - Screenshots should hide real account names, keys, patient information, and server details. Pre-task checklist - [ ] The workspace or project copy is correct - [ ] A Git baseline has been recorded - [ ] The Runtime and file access range match the task - [ ] Output directories and overwrite policy are clear - [ ] Boundaries for network, installation, sign-in, and upload are clear - [ ] Acceptance and recovery methods are clear

en.title: Troubleshooting
en.description: Diagnose SciForge problems across five layers: interface, Runtime, model access, permissions, and external services.
en.body: Troubleshooting First determine which layer the problem is in, so you do not change models, the Runtime, permissions, and workspace settings all at once. Five-layer quick diagnosis Layer Check first --- --- App interface Whether SciForge started correctly and the current workspace is the right one Runtime Whether Codex, Claude Code, or DSH is currently selected, whether the command can be found, and whether sign-in is valid Model access Whether the Model API or Coding Plan is fully configured Permissions and tools File access range, operation confirmations, Computer Use run status, and system permissions External services Whether the cloud, models, and external tools are connected properly; whether the remote workspace is still connected Runtime shows as disconnected 1. Open Settings → AI assistant and confirm the current Runtime. 2. In your system terminal, check whether codex , claude , or dsh can be found. 3. If automatic detection fails, enter the absolute path to the executable. 4. After changing it, reconnect or start a new session. 5. Do not expect an automatic switch to another Runtime after a failure. Runtime is connected but the model does not respond - Confirm whether you are using a Model API or a Coding Plan. - A Model API requires a Base URL, API Key, and model name that match completely. - A Coding Plan requires a valid official sign-in state. - The current Coding Plan path supports Codex; if you select Claude Code, configure the Model API. - Do not put a Provider API key in the Runtime sign-in field. - Test with a minimal prompt that reads no files first, then investigate tools and the sandbox. A read-only task still changes files 1. Stop the task immediately. 2. Compare git status --short before and after the task. 3. Have the installed and authorized Change Inspector inspect the current session changes and compare them with the actual files. 4. Confirm the executor, whether settings were applied, and whether you approved expanded permissions; Claude Plan mode is not the same as the Codex read-only sandbox. 5. Check whether tests, interpreters, MCP, remote tools, or Computer Use wrote anything. Files ignored by Git need a separate check. 6. Do not automatically delete user changes that existed before the task. Scientific files are not understood - Check the extension, file version, and workspace reference. - Do not paste large files directly into a prompt. - Confirm in the file preview whether the format is supported; look for size limits or read errors. - When the current Provider does not support a binary format, it should explicitly degrade or stop rather than guess at the content. Evidence DAG or dossier is empty These panels do not generate evidence automatically from an empty session. First have the task explicitly record the research question, inputs, methods, claims, sources, artifacts, and limitations, then refresh the corresponding panel. The remote workspace is interrupted - In the workspace location picker, confirm the remote session state (remote, reconnecting, offline, or connection error). - Use Reconnect on a session that is offline or has errored; if reconnecting fails, switch back to a local workspace and continue local tasks. - Check whether the remote command is still running, and do not resubmit a long computation when the state is unknown. - After the connection is restored, check the logs, output files, and return codes. Include when filing an issue - SciForge version and operating system - The selected Runtime and how model access is configured - Workspace type: local or remote - Minimal reproduction steps and the time it occurred - Redacted logs or screenshots - Expected behavior and actual behavior Before submitting, remove API keys, Authorization headers, account names, server information, sample privacy data, and real sensitive paths.
